chapters.title: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates

learn.hook: How do you tell a friend exactly where your seat is in a cinema hall? Row and seat number! Two numbers can pin down any spot.
points: Two perpendicular number lines make the Cartesian plane: the horizontal x-axis and the vertical y-axis.
The axes meet at the origin O, whose coordinates are (0, 0).
Every point is named by an ordered pair (x, y). The x-coordinate (abscissa) tells how far left or right; the y-coordinate (ordinate) tells how far up or down.
Order matters: (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different points.
A point on the x-axis has y = 0, and a point on the y-axis has x = 0.

example.q: Point P is 4 units to the right of the y-axis and 3 units below the x-axis. Write its coordinates.
steps: Right of the y-axis means x is positive: x = 4
Below the x-axis means y is negative: y = −3

learn.reallife: Maps on your phone use latitude and longitude, which is a coordinate system on the Earth. Chess squares like e4 work the same way.

games.title: True or false?
items: (3, 7) and (7, 3) are the same point
Order matters: the first number is x and the second is y, so these are two different points.
Every point on the y-axis has x-coordinate 0
On the y-axis you have not moved left or right at all, so x = 0.
The point (0, −4) lies on the x-axis
Its x-coordinate is 0, so it lies on the y-axis, 4 units below the origin.
The x-axis and the y-axis are perpendicular to each other
The two axes cross at a right angle at the origin.
The ordinate of (6, −1) is 6
The ordinate is the y-coordinate, which is −1.

quiz.q: In the point (−6, 2), what is the abscissa?
quiz.explain: The abscissa is the x-coordinate, the first number of the ordered pair.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up abscissa (x) and ordinate (y), or drops the negative sign

quiz.q: What is the ordinate of the point (5, −9)?
quiz.explain: The ordinate is the y-coordinate, the second number of the pair.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ordinate is the first number, or ignores the sign

quiz.q: Which point lies on the y-axis?
quiz.explain: Points on the y-axis have x-coordinate 0, so (0, 7) is on the y-axis, 7 units above the origin.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a 0 in the y place puts the point on the y-axis

quiz.q: Where do the x-axis and the y-axis meet?
quiz.explain: The two axes cross at the origin, where both coordinates are zero.
quiz.mistake: Thinks counting starts at 1 on the axes

quiz.q: Arjun stands at the origin, walks 3 units left and then 5 units up. What are his coordinates now?
quiz.explain: Left makes x negative, so x = −3. Up makes y positive, so y = 5. He is at (−3, 5).
quiz.mistake: Forgets that moving left gives a negative x-coordinate

quiz.q: Point A is at (4, 0). How far is A from the origin?
quiz.explain: A is on the x-axis, 4 steps to the right of the origin.
steps: A lies on the x-axis because y = 0
quiz.mistake: Reads the 0 as the distance

quiz.q: Which statement about the point (2, 9) is correct?
options: It is 2 units from the x-axis and 9 units from the y-axis
It is 2 units from the y-axis and 9 units from the x-axis
quiz.explain: The x-coordinate 2 tells how far the point is from the y-axis; the y-coordinate 9 tells how far it is from the x-axis.
quiz.mistake: Matches the x-coordinate with the x-axis distance instead of the y-axis distance

quiz.q: How far is the point (−5, 3) from the y-axis?
quiz.explain: Distance from the y-axis is the size of the x-coordinate. A distance is never negative, so it is 5 units.
quiz.mistake: Uses the y-coordinate, or gives a negative distance

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: "Why do you need TWO numbers to name a point? Isn't one number enough?"
teach.praise: Chirp! One number for across, one for up or down, and the order matters. Now I can find any spot!
teach.nudge: But which number do I use first, the across one or the up one?

learn.hook: A treasure map says: from the big banyan tree, walk 3 steps east and 4 steps north. Plotting points is exactly that!
points: To plot (a, b), start at the origin. Move a units along the x-axis: right if a is positive, left if a is negative.
From there move b units parallel to the y-axis: up if b is positive, down if b is negative. Mark the point.
Points with the same y-coordinate lie on one horizontal line; points with the same x-coordinate lie on one vertical line.
On graph paper choose a scale, for example 1 cm = 1 unit, and use it on both axes.
Length of a horizontal segment = difference of the x-coordinates; length of a vertical segment = difference of the y-coordinates.

example.q: Plot A(2, 3), B(−2, 3), C(−2, −1) and D(2, −1). What shape do they make, and what is its perimeter?
steps: AB is horizontal (same y): length = 2 − (−2) = 4 units
BC is vertical (same x): length = 3 − (−1) = 4 units
Similarly CD = 4 and DA = 4, and the sides meet at right angles
So ABCD is a square; perimeter = 4 × 4 = 16 units
example.answer: A square of side 4 units, perimeter 16 units

learn.reallife: Rangoli artists often mark dots on a grid first. Each dot is really a point with coordinates!

games.prompt: Put the steps in the right order

Move 3 units to the left along the x-axis
From there move 4 units up
Mark the point and label it (−3, 4)

quiz.q: To plot (−4, 6), which move do you make first from the origin?
quiz.explain: The x-coordinate comes first. It is −4, so move 4 units to the left, then 6 units up.
quiz.mistake: Starts with the y-coordinate or ignores the negative sign

quiz.q: Which point lies on the same horizontal line as (3, −2)?
quiz.explain: A horizontal line keeps the y-coordinate the same. (−5, −2) has y = −2, just like (3, −2).
quiz.mistake: Keeps the x-coordinate the same, which gives a vertical line

quiz.q: Kabir plots P(1, 2) and Q(1, 8). What is the length of PQ?
quiz.explain: P and Q have the same x-coordinate, so PQ is vertical. Its length is the difference of the y-coordinates.
steps: Same x, so PQ is vertical
quiz.mistake: Adds the y-coordinates instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Riya draws a rectangle with corners (0, 0), (6, 0), (6, 4) and (0, 4). What is its area?
quiz.explain: The length along the x-axis is 6 and the height along the y-axis is 4, so the area is 6 × 4.
quiz.mistake: Finds the perimeter (20) or adds the sides (10) instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Three corners of a square are (1, 1), (5, 1) and (5, 5). What is the fourth corner?
quiz.explain: The side from (1, 1) to (5, 1) has length 4. The missing corner is 4 units above (1, 1), at (1, 5).
quiz.mistake: Swaps x and y or continues the pattern in the wrong direction

quiz.q: Meena reads a point on a graph: it is 3 units below the x-axis and 7 units to the left of the y-axis. Which point is it?
quiz.explain: 7 units left of the y-axis gives x = −7; 3 units below the x-axis gives y = −3.
quiz.mistake: Writes the numbers in the order they were read instead of (x, y)

quiz.q: On graph paper Joseph uses the scale 1 cm = 2 units. How far along the x-axis must he move to plot (10, 0)?
quiz.explain: Each centimetre stands for 2 units, so 10 units need 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by the scale instead of dividing

quiz.q: Points A(−3, 2) and B(4, 2) are plotted. What is the length of AB?
quiz.explain: Same y-coordinate, so AB is horizontal. Length = 4 − (−3) = 7 units.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 3 from 4 without handling the negative sign, getting 1

teach.ask: Gappu holds a pencil: "I want to put a dot at (−2, 5). Where do I even start?"
teach.praise: Start at the origin, go across first, then up or down. My dot landed perfectly!
teach.nudge: Which way do I go first, and does the minus sign change the direction?

learn.hook: The two axes cut the plane like a roti cut into four pieces. Each piece has its own sign pattern!
points: The axes divide the plane into four quadrants, numbered I, II, III, IV going anticlockwise from the top right.
Signs of (x, y): Quadrant I (+, +), Quadrant II (−, +), Quadrant III (−, −), Quadrant IV (+, −).
A point on an axis does not belong to any quadrant.
Distance between two points: across distance and up distance form the two shorter sides of a right triangle, so by Pythagoras, distance = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].
Distance of (x, y) from the origin = √(x² + y²).

example.q: Find the distance between A(1, 2) and B(4, 6).

learn.reallife: Delivery apps estimate the straight-line distance between your home and a shop using coordinates and this very formula.

quiz.q: In which quadrant does (−5, 8) lie?
quiz.explain: x is negative and y is positive: (−, +) is Quadrant II, the top-left part.
quiz.mistake: Numbers the quadrants clockwise instead of anticlockwise

quiz.q: A point has a negative x-coordinate and a negative y-coordinate. Which quadrant is it in?
quiz.explain: (−, −) means left of the y-axis and below the x-axis: the bottom-left part, Quadrant III.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Quadrant III with Quadrant IV

quiz.q: Which point is in Quadrant IV?
quiz.explain: Quadrant IV has positive x and negative y. Only (3, −2) has the sign pattern (+, −).
quiz.mistake: Thinks a point on an axis such as (0, −2) belongs to a quadrant

quiz.q: Where does the point (0, −6) lie?
options: On the y-axis, in no quadrant
quiz.explain: Its x-coordinate is 0, so it sits on the y-axis. Points on the axes are not in any quadrant.
quiz.mistake: Assigns a quadrant to a point that lies on an axis

quiz.q: Find the distance between A(2, 1) and B(8, 9).
quiz.explain: Across 6 and up 8 form the legs of a right triangle; the distance is the hypotenuse.
quiz.mistake: Adds 6 and 8 instead of using Pythagoras, or forgets the square root

quiz.q: How far is the point (−5, −12) from the origin?
quiz.explain: Use √(x² + y²). Squaring removes the negative signs.
quiz.mistake: Adds the coordinates directly instead of squaring them

quiz.q: On a town map (1 unit = 1 km), Harpreet's house is at (−3, 4) and her school is at (5, 4). What is the straight distance between them?
quiz.explain: Both points have y = 4, so the line joining them is horizontal. Subtract the x-coordinates.
quiz.mistake: Computes 5 − 3 = 2, forgetting that subtracting a negative means adding

quiz.q: The point (a, 3) lies in Quadrant II. Which value can a be?
quiz.explain: Quadrant II needs a negative x-coordinate. Only −4 is negative. (a = 0 would put the point on the y-axis.)
quiz.mistake: Forgets that Quadrant II has negative x-values

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his feathers: "How can I tell which quadrant a point is in without drawing it?"
teach.praise: Just look at the signs of x and y! (+, +) is I, then go anticlockwise. Easy peasy!
teach.nudge: Do the signs of x and y help? And which way do we count the quadrants?

learn.hook: An auto fare of ₹30 plus ₹15 for every km grows by the same amount each km. That steady growth is a linear polynomial!
points: A linear polynomial in x has the form ax + b, where a and b are numbers and a ≠ 0.
Its degree is 1: the highest power of x is x¹. Terms like x², 1/x or √x are not allowed.
a is the coefficient of x and b is the constant term.
To evaluate p(x) at x = k, replace x by k: p(k) = ak + b.
Each time x goes up by 1, the value of ax + b changes by exactly a.

example.q: A taxi charges ₹50 to start plus ₹12 per km. Write the fare for x km as a polynomial and find the fare for 8 km.

learn.reallife: Electricity bills, mobile data plans and taxi fares often have a fixed charge plus a charge per unit: a linear polynomial.

quiz.q: Which of these is a linear polynomial?
quiz.explain: 4x − 1 has the form ax + b with highest power of x equal to 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any expression with x is linear, even with x², x³ or x in the denominator

quiz.q: If p(x) = 3x − 7, find p(4).
quiz.explain: Replace x by 4 and simplify.
quiz.mistake: Adds 7 instead of subtracting it, getting 19

quiz.q: What is the degree of the polynomial 6 − 2x?
quiz.explain: The highest power of x is x¹, so the degree is 1.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the degree with a coefficient or the constant term

quiz.q: Aisha's phone plan costs ₹99 fixed plus ₹2 per GB of data. Which polynomial gives the cost for x GB?
quiz.explain: The ₹2 is paid for each GB, so it multiplies x. The ₹99 is paid once, so it is the constant.
quiz.mistake: Attaches x to the fixed charge instead of the per-unit charge

quiz.q: For p(x) = 5x + 2, find p(−3).
quiz.mistake: Drops the negative sign when multiplying by −3

quiz.q: At a sports shop the price of x cricket balls is p(x) = 150x rupees. What is p(4) − p(3)?
quiz.explain: One extra ball adds the coefficient of x, ₹150, to the price.
quiz.mistake: Gives p(4) or p(3) instead of their difference

quiz.q: Which expression is NOT a linear polynomial?
quiz.explain: x(x + 1) = x² + x has degree 2, so it is not linear. x/3 + 1 is linear because x/3 = (1/3)x.
quiz.mistake: Thinks dividing x by a number makes it non-linear, or misses the hidden x²

quiz.q: If p(x) = ax + 4 and p(2) = 10, what is a?
quiz.explain: Put x = 2: 2a + 4 = 10, so 2a = 6 and a = 3.
quiz.mistake: Divides 10 by 2 without first subtracting 4

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "What makes a polynomial 'linear'? It sounds like a line, but it is just letters and numbers!"
teach.praise: Highest power of x is one, like ax + b. And it really does make a line on a graph. Super!
teach.nudge: What is the highest power of x allowed in a linear polynomial?

learn.hook: Put a linear polynomial on a graph and something magical happens: every point falls in one perfectly straight line!
points: To graph y = ax + b, make a table: choose some x-values, work out y, plot the points (x, y) and join them.
The graph of a linear polynomial is always a straight line. Two points are enough to draw it; a third point is a good check.
b is where the line cuts the y-axis: the point (0, b).
a is the slope: when x increases by 1, y changes by a. If a > 0 the line rises; if a < 0 it falls.
Lines with the same a (same slope) are parallel.

example.q: Draw the graph of y = 2x + 1 using x = 0, 1, 2.
steps: Plot and join: a rising straight line cutting the y-axis at (0, 1); y goes up by 2 for each step of 1 in x

learn.reallife: A plot of distance against time for a train moving at steady speed is a straight line; the steeper the line, the faster the train.

quiz.q: What does the graph of y = 4x − 3 look like?
quiz.explain: y = 4x − 3 is a linear polynomial, and every linear polynomial has a straight-line graph.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a negative constant bends the graph

quiz.q: Where does the line y = 3x + 5 cut the y-axis?
quiz.explain: On the y-axis x = 0, so y = 3 × 0 + 5 = 5. The point is (0, 5).
quiz.mistake: Writes the intercept as (5, 0), swapping x and y

quiz.q: For y = 2x − 1, what is y when x = 4?
quiz.explain: Substitute x = 4: 2 × 4 − 1 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Adds 1 instead of subtracting it

quiz.q: Which line falls as x increases?
quiz.explain: A line falls when its slope (the coefficient of x) is negative. Only y = −3x + 1 has a negative slope.
quiz.mistake: Looks at the sign of the constant term instead of the coefficient of x

quiz.q: On the graph of y = 5x + 2, by how much does y increase when x goes up by 1?
quiz.explain: The coefficient of x is the slope. Each step of 1 in x adds 5 to y.
quiz.mistake: Chooses the constant term instead of the slope

quiz.q: Which point lies on the line y = −2x + 6?
quiz.explain: Check each point: for x = 1, y = −2 + 6 = 4, so (1, 4) is on the line.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign on the slope

quiz.q: Kabir has ₹100 and saves ₹20 every week, so his savings after x weeks are y = 20x + 100. After how many weeks will he have ₹260?
quiz.mistake: Divides 260 by 20 without removing the starting ₹100

teach.nudge: How many points do I really need, and what shape will I get?

learn.hook: A lemonade stall makes a loss at first and a profit later. The exact moment it breaks even is a zero of a polynomial!
points: A zero of p(x) is a value of x that makes p(x) = 0.
For p(x) = ax + b with a ≠ 0, solve ax + b = 0 to get the zero x = −b/a.
A linear polynomial has exactly one zero.
On the graph, the zero is where the line crosses the x-axis: the point (−b/a, 0).
To check a zero, substitute it: the answer must come out as 0.

example.q: Find the zero of p(x) = 3x − 12 and say where its graph meets the x-axis.
steps: The line meets the x-axis at (4, 0)
example.answer: x = 4; the graph crosses the x-axis at (4, 0)

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers find the break-even number of items, where profit is exactly zero, by finding the zero of a profit polynomial.

games.title: Match each polynomial with its zero

quiz.q: What is the zero of p(x) = x − 6?
quiz.explain: x − 6 = 0 gives x = 6. Check: 6 − 6 = 0.
quiz.mistake: Takes the constant with its sign (−6) as the zero

quiz.q: Find the zero of 4x + 20.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that moving +20 across makes it −20

quiz.q: Where does the graph of y = 2x − 10 cross the x-axis?
quiz.explain: On the x-axis y = 0, so 2x − 10 = 0 and x = 5. The crossing point is (5, 0).
quiz.mistake: Gives the y-intercept (0, −10) instead of the x-axis crossing

quiz.q: How many zeros does a linear polynomial ax + b (with a ≠ 0) have?
quiz.explain: A non-horizontal straight line crosses the x-axis exactly once, at x = −b/a.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up linear polynomials with quadratics, which can have two zeros

quiz.q: Is x = 3 a zero of p(x) = 3x − 9?
quiz.explain: p(3) = 3 × 3 − 9 = 0, so 3 is a zero.
quiz.mistake: Substitutes x = 0 instead of x = 3

quiz.q: Arjun's lemonade stall makes a profit of p(x) = 5x − 150 rupees when he sells x glasses. How many glasses must he sell to break even (zero profit)?
quiz.explain: Break even means p(x) = 0: 5x = 150, so x = 30.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts or multiplies instead of dividing 150 by 5

quiz.q: The zero of 3x + k is 2. What is k?
quiz.explain: Since 2 is a zero, 3 × 2 + k = 0, so k = −6.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the sign and writes k = 6

quiz.q: What is the zero of p(x) = 2x + 3?
quiz.mistake: Divides the wrong way round (−2/3) or loses the minus sign

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: "What is a 'zero' of a polynomial? Is it just the number 0?"
teach.praise: Oh! It is the x that makes the polynomial equal zero, where the line crosses the x-axis. Tweet-tastic!
teach.nudge: Is the zero a value of x or a value of p(x)? And where can I see it on the graph?

learn.hook: Some numbers can be written as a neat fraction. Others, like √2, refuse to be caught by any fraction at all, no matter how hard you try!
points: A rational number can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Examples: 3 = 3/1, −0.5 = −1/2, 0 = 0/1.
Every natural number, whole number and integer is also a rational number.
An irrational number cannot be written as p/q. Examples: √2, √3, √5 and π.
If n is a natural number that is not a perfect square, then √n is irrational. But √16 = 4 is rational.
Between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many more rational numbers; their average is always one of them.

example.q: Find three rational numbers between 1/3 and 1/2.
steps: Multiply top and bottom by 2 to make room: 8/24 and 12/24

learn.reallife: The diagonal of a square tile of side 1 m is √2 m long. A carpenter can measure it closely, but never as an exact fraction!

games.title: True or false?
items: Every integer is a rational number
Any integer n can be written as n/1.
π is exactly equal to 22/7
22/7 is only a handy approximation. π is irrational, so no fraction equals it exactly.
The square root of every natural number is irrational
√9 = 3 and √25 = 5 are rational. Only non-perfect squares give irrational roots.
0 is a rational number
0 = 0/1, which is in the form p/q with q ≠ 0.
The sum of two irrational numbers is always irrational
√2 + (−√2) = 0, and 0 is rational.
3√2 is irrational
A non-zero rational number times an irrational number is always irrational.

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is irrational?
quiz.explain: 11 is not a perfect square, so √11 cannot be written as p/q. √25 = 5, 0.6 = 3/5 and −7/3 are all rational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every number with a root sign is irrational

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is rational?
quiz.explain: √36 = 6 = 6/1, which is rational. The others cannot be written as fractions.
quiz.mistake: Sees the root sign and assumes the number must be irrational

quiz.q: Which number lies between 2/5 and 3/5?
quiz.explain: 2/5 = 0.4 and 3/5 = 0.6. Their average is 1/2 = 0.5, which lies between them.
quiz.mistake: Compares only numerators or denominators instead of the whole fractions

quiz.q: Meena's calculator shows √2 = 1.414213562. Which statement is correct?
options: The display is only an approximation; √2 is irrational and its decimals never end or repeat
√2 is rational because the calculator shows a decimal
quiz.explain: √2 is irrational. A calculator can only show a few digits, so what you see is a rounded value.
quiz.mistake: Believes a calculator display is always exact

quiz.q: What kind of number is 2 + √3?
quiz.explain: A rational number plus an irrational number is always irrational. If 2 + √3 were p/q, then √3 would be p/q − 2, a fraction, which is impossible.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding a whole number makes the result rational

quiz.q: What is √2 × √8?
quiz.explain: √2 × √8 = √(2 × 8) = √16 = 4. Two irrational numbers can multiply to give a rational one.
quiz.mistake: Adds the numbers under the root instead of multiplying them

quiz.q: How many rational numbers lie between 1 and 2?
quiz.explain: You can always find another rational number between any two, for example 1.5, 1.25, 1.125, ... so the list never ends.
quiz.mistake: Counts only decimals with one decimal place (1.1 to 1.9)

quiz.q: Which of these is a rational number even though it has a root sign?
quiz.explain: √(9/16) = √9 / √16 = 3/4, which is rational.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every square root is irrational

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: "What is the difference between a rational and an irrational number? They both look like numbers to me!"
teach.praise: So a rational number can be written as a fraction p/q, and an irrational one like √2 or π never can. Clear as a blue sky!
teach.nudge: Can every number be written as a fraction? Can you give me an example that cannot?

learn.hook: √2 is not a fraction, yet you can mark it exactly on a number line with just a ruler and a compass. Here is the trick!
points: Rational and irrational numbers together make up the real numbers.
Every real number is a point on the number line, and every point on the line is a real number. The line has no gaps.
To mark √2: draw a right triangle on the line with legs 1 and 1. Its hypotenuse is √(1 + 1) = √2; swing an arc from 0 with that length.
In the same way, legs 2 and 1 give √5, and legs √2 and 1 give √3.
To compare roots, compare squares: √10 < 3.2 because 10 < 3.2² = 10.24.

example.q: Show how to mark √5 on the number line.
steps: Mark O at 0 and A at 2 on the number line
At A, draw AB = 1 unit perpendicular to the line
With centre O and radius OB, draw an arc to cut the line at P. Then OP = √5 ≈ 2.24
example.answer: P is the point √5, a little to the right of 2.2

learn.reallife: A ruler with marks only at whole and half centimetres still contains the point √2 cm: every length you can draw is a real number.

quiz.q: Between which two whole numbers does √20 lie?
quiz.explain: 4² = 16 and 5² = 25. Since 16 < 20 < 25, √20 lies between 4 and 5.
quiz.mistake: Looks at numbers near 20 instead of the squares near 20

quiz.q: To mark √2 on the number line, which right triangle do you draw?
quiz.explain: With legs 1 and 1 the hypotenuse is √(1² + 1²) = √2.
quiz.mistake: Uses legs 1 and 2, which give √5 instead

quiz.q: Which is greater, √10 or 3.2?
quiz.explain: Compare squares: (√10)² = 10 and 3.2² = 10.24. Since 10 < 10.24, 3.2 is greater.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a number with a root sign must be bigger, or guesses √10 ≈ 3.3

quiz.q: From 0 on a number line, Arjun marks 3 units, draws a 2-unit perpendicular there and swings the hypotenuse down onto the line. Which number does he get?
quiz.explain: The hypotenuse is √(3² + 2²) = √(9 + 4) = √13.
quiz.mistake: Adds the legs (5) or forgets to take the square root (13)

quiz.q: Which statement about the number line is true?
options: Only rational numbers can be marked on it
√2 cannot be shown on it because its decimals never end
Every point on it stands for a real number
There are gaps that no number fills
quiz.explain: The real numbers fill the whole line: each point is a real number and each real number has a point.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a number must have a finite decimal to have a place on the line

quiz.q: Which list is in increasing order?
quiz.mistake: Thinks √2 is bigger than 1.5

quiz.q: Riya jumps √9 units and then √16 more units to the right of 0. Where does she land?
quiz.explain: √9 = 3 and √16 = 4, so she lands at 3 + 4 = 7. Note that √9 + √16 is not the same as √(9 + 16) = 5.
quiz.mistake: Writes √9 + √16 = √25 = 5, adding under one root

quiz.q: √50 is closest to which value?
quiz.explain: 7² = 49, so √50 is just a little more than 7. In fact 7.07² ≈ 49.98.
quiz.mistake: Halves the number instead of taking its square root

teach.ask: Gappu holds a compass: "How can I put √2 on a number line if I can't even write it as a fraction?"
teach.praise: A right triangle with sides 1 and 1, then swing the hypotenuse down with a compass. √2 has a home on the line!
teach.nudge: What shape do I draw first, and how do I bring its long side down onto the line?

learn.hook: Divide 1 by 8 and the division stops. Divide 1 by 7 and the digits 142857 go round and round forever. Why?
points: The decimal expansion of a rational number either terminates (ends), like 3/8 = 0.375, or is non-terminating and recurring (repeats), like 1/3 = 0.333...
A fraction in lowest terms terminates only if its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. So 7/20 terminates, but 5/12 repeats.
An irrational number has a decimal expansion that is non-terminating and non-recurring: it never ends and never settles into a repeating block.
A repeating decimal can be turned back into p/q. For 0.777..., let x = 0.777...; then 10x = 7.777..., so 9x = 7 and x = 7/9.
The repeating block is shown with a bar on top, for example 0.27 with a bar on 27 means 0.272727...

example.q: Write 0.474747... (47 repeating) in the form p/q.
steps: Two digits repeat, so multiply by 100: 100x = 47.474747...

learn.reallife: When ₹100 is shared equally among 3 friends, each share is ₹33.333..., so in real life we round it to ₹33.33.

games.title: What kind of decimal?
items: π

items.q: 0.454545... (45 repeating) as a fraction in lowest terms

quiz.q: What is the decimal expansion of 7/8?
quiz.explain: 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875. The division ends because 8 = 2³ has only the prime factor 2.
quiz.mistake: Just writes the numerator and denominator side by side after the point

quiz.q: Which fraction has a terminating decimal expansion?
quiz.explain: 40 = 2³ × 5 has only 2s and 5s, so 11/40 = 0.275 terminates. 7, 12 = 2² × 3 and 9 = 3² all contain other primes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an even denominator always gives a terminating decimal

quiz.q: The decimal expansion of an irrational number is:
quiz.explain: If the decimal ended or repeated, the number could be written as p/q and would be rational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any decimal that goes on forever is irrational, even if it repeats

quiz.q: Write 0.777... (7 repeating) as a fraction.
quiz.explain: Let x = 0.777...; 10x = 7.777...; subtracting gives 9x = 7, so x = 7/9.
quiz.mistake: Writes 7/10, treating the repeating decimal as if it stopped after one digit

quiz.q: Write 0.363636... (36 repeating) in lowest terms.
quiz.explain: Two digits repeat: 100x − x = 36, so x = 36/99 = 4/11.
quiz.mistake: Uses 90 instead of 99 when two digits repeat

quiz.q: 1/7 = 0.142857142857... How many digits are in its repeating block?
quiz.explain: The block 142857 repeats, and it has 6 digits.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the block length must equal the denominator 7

quiz.q: Aisha shares ₹100 equally among 3 friends. Which describes 100/3 as a decimal?
quiz.explain: 100 ÷ 3 = 33.333..., with 3 repeating forever. It repeats, so it is rational, not irrational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the rounded money value is the exact answer

quiz.q: Which number is irrational?
quiz.explain: In 0.1211211121111... the number of 1s keeps growing, so no fixed block repeats. It never ends and never repeats, so it is irrational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any long decimal is irrational without checking for a repeating block

teach.ask: Gappu taps the calculator: "Some decimals stop, some repeat and some go wild. How can I tell which numbers are rational from their decimals?"
teach.praise: Decimals that end or repeat belong to rational numbers; decimals that never end and never repeat are irrational. Tweet-tastic!
teach.nudge: What happens to the decimal of 1/3 compared with √2? Does one of them repeat?

learn.hook: Can you find 103 × 103 in your head in five seconds? With the right identity, you can!
points: An identity is an equality that is true for every value of the variables, unlike an equation such as x + 2 = 5, which is true for only one value.
(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². Picture a square of side a + b split into an a × a square, a b × b square and two a × b rectangles.
(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
(x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab.

example.q: Find 103² without long multiplication.
steps: 103 = 100 + 3, so use (a + b)² with a = 100, b = 3

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers who multiply mentally often use these tricks: 49 × 51 = 50² − 1² = 2499.

games.title: Match each product with its expansion

quiz.q: Expand (x + 7)².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the middle term 2ab and writes x² + 49

quiz.q: Use (a − b)² to find 98².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the middle term (getting 9804) or drops the + b² (getting 9600)

quiz.q: Find 47 × 53 using an identity.
quiz.mistake: Adds 9 instead of subtracting it

quiz.q: Expand (3a − 2b)².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the middle term, writing 6ab

quiz.q: Expand (x + 4)(x − 9).
quiz.explain: Use (x + a)(x + b) with a = 4, b = −9: a + b = −5 and ab = −36.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign of the middle term wrong

quiz.q: If a + b = 10 and ab = 21, find a² + b².
quiz.explain: (a + b)² = a² + b² + 2ab, so a² + b² = 100 − 42 = 58. Check with a = 3, b = 7: 9 + 49 = 58.
quiz.mistake: Takes a² + b² = (a + b)², forgetting the 2ab

quiz.q: Which of these is an identity (true for every value of x)?
quiz.explain: (x + 1)² = x² + 2x + 1 holds for every x. The others are true only for some values (or are false in general).
quiz.mistake: Confuses an equation that is true for one value with an identity

quiz.q: Find 1002² − 998².
quiz.mistake: Uses only a − b and forgets to multiply by a + b

teach.ask: Gappu groans: "Why isn't (a + b)² just a² + b²? That looks so much simpler!"
teach.praise: Of course! The big square also has two a × b rectangles, so (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² for every value. I won't forget 2ab now!
teach.nudge: If you draw a square of side a + b, what pieces do you see besides a² and b²?

learn.hook: 11³ = 1331 and 101³ = 1030301. Patterns like these come straight from the cube identities!
points: (a + b)³ = a³ + b³ + 3ab(a + b) = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³.
(a − b)³ = a³ − b³ − 3ab(a − b) = a³ − 3a²b + 3ab² − b³.
a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) and a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²).
(a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca.
a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca). So if a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc.

example.q: Find 11³ using (a + b)³.

learn.reallife: Volumes of cube-shaped boxes grow as a cube. If each side of a 10 cm box grows by 1 cm, (a + b)³ shows exactly how much extra space you get.

games.title: Cube check
items: (a + b)³ = a³ + b³
You also need the term 3ab(a + b). Try a = b = 1: 8 is not 2.
a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²)
Multiply out the right side and the middle terms cancel, leaving a³ − b³.
If a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc
This follows from a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(...), which is 0 when a + b + c = 0.
(a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c²
The cross terms 2ab + 2bc + 2ca are missing.
Use (a − b)³ = a³ − 3a²b + 3ab² − b³ with a = x, b = 1.

items.text: (a + b)³ = a³ + b³ + ___
(x + y + z)² = x² + y² + z² + ___

quiz.q: Expand (x + 2)³.
quiz.explain: a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³ with a = x, b = 2 gives x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.
quiz.mistake: Cubes each term separately and drops the middle terms

quiz.q: Find 102³ using an identity.
quiz.mistake: Uses 3ab instead of 3ab(a + b), getting 1000608, or forgets the middle part entirely

quiz.q: Find (−12)³ + 7³ + 5³ without cubing each number.
quiz.explain: −12 + 7 + 5 = 0, so the sum of cubes equals 3abc = 3 × (−12) × 7 × 5 = −1260.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the answer is 0 because a + b + c = 0, or drops the negative sign

quiz.q: Expand (x + y + 2)².
quiz.explain: Use a² + b² + c² + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca with c = 2: 2bc = 4y and 2ca = 4x.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the cross terms

quiz.q: Factorise x³ − 27.
quiz.explain: a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) with a = x, b = 3.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the signs of the sum-of-cubes and difference-of-cubes identities

quiz.q: If x + y = 5 and xy = 6, find x³ + y³.
quiz.mistake: Thinks x³ + y³ = (x + y)³

quiz.q: Expand (2x − 1)³.
quiz.explain: (a − b)³ = a³ − 3a²b + 3ab² − b³ with a = 2x, b = 1: 8x³ − 12x² + 6x − 1.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to cube the 2 in 2x, or gets the alternating signs wrong

quiz.q: If a + b + c = 9 and ab + bc + ca = 26, find a² + b² + c².
quiz.explain: a² + b² + c² = (a + b + c)² − 2(ab + bc + ca) = 81 − 52 = 29.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 26 instead of 2 × 26

teach.ask: Gappu counts on his feathers: "Why does (a + b)³ have so many terms? Can't I just cube a and cube b?"
teach.praise: (a + b)³ is (a + b) multiplied three times, so the extra terms 3a²b + 3ab² appear. Just a³ + b³ is not enough!
teach.nudge: What do you get if you multiply (a + b)² by (a + b) once more?

learn.hook: Expanding is like opening a gift box; factorising is packing it back. Identities show you how the box was folded!
points: To factorise means to write an expression as a product of simpler expressions.
Always take out a common factor first: 3x² − 75 = 3(x² − 25).
Look for patterns: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b); a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)²; a² − 2ab + b² = (a − b)².
For x² + px + q, find two numbers with sum p and product q: x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4).
a³ + b³ and a³ − b³ have their own factor forms. Always check by expanding your answer.

example.q: Factorise 4x² − 12x + 9.
steps: Middle term: 2 × 2x × 3 = 12x, with a minus sign
So it matches a² − 2ab + b² with a = 2x, b = 3

learn.reallife: If a rectangular rangoli has area x² + 9x + 20, factorising tells you possible side lengths: (x + 4) and (x + 5).

games.title: Match each expression with its factors
Factorise 3x² − 75
items: Take out the common factor 3: 3(x² − 25)
Spot a difference of squares: x² − 5²
Use a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b)
Write the answer 3(x − 5)(x + 5)

quiz.q: Factorise 9y² − 16.
quiz.explain: 9y² − 16 = (3y)² − 4², a difference of squares.
quiz.mistake: Writes a difference of squares as a perfect square

quiz.q: Factorise x² + 8x + 16.
quiz.mistake: Finds numbers with product 16 but ignores the sum 8

quiz.q: Factorise x² − 7x + 12.
quiz.explain: We need two numbers with sum −7 and product 12: −3 and −4.
quiz.mistake: Uses + signs even though the middle term is negative

quiz.q: Factorise 2x² − 18 completely.
quiz.explain: Take out 2 to get 2(x² − 9), then x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3).
quiz.mistake: Stops after taking out the common factor

quiz.q: Use factorisation to find 87² − 13².
quiz.mistake: Computes (87 − 13)² = 5476 instead

quiz.q: Factorise x² + x − 20.
quiz.explain: Two numbers with product −20 and sum +1 are 5 and −4.
quiz.mistake: Puts the signs the wrong way round, giving a sum of −1

quiz.q: Factorise 27a³ − 8.
quiz.mistake: Uses a minus sign in the second bracket, mixing it up with a³ + b³

quiz.q: A rectangular rangoli has area x² + 9x + 20 square units. One side is (x + 4). What is the other side?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 4 from 20 instead of dividing, or uses the coefficient 9

teach.ask: Gappu stares at x² − 49: "How do I break this into factors? Where do I start?"
teach.praise: First take out anything common, then match a pattern like a² − b², and finally multiply back to check. x² − 49 = (x − 7)(x + 7)!
teach.nudge: Is 49 a square number? Which identity has a minus sign between two squares?

chapters.title: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round

learn.hook: A giant wheel at the Dussehra mela lifts you up, brings you down, and does it again and again. Things that repeat like this are called periodic!
points: A motion is periodic if it repeats itself exactly after a fixed interval of time.
The time for one complete cycle is the period. The number of cycles in one unit of time is the frequency: frequency = 1 ÷ period.
Examples: the swing of a pendulum, the hands of a clock, a giant wheel, days of the week, phases of the Moon.
To find where a periodic motion is after a long time, divide the time by the period and look at the remainder.
The graph of height against time for a seat on a giant wheel is a smooth wave that rises and falls again and again.

example.q: A giant wheel takes 4 minutes for one full turn. Riya's seat is at the bottom at time 0. Where is it after 22 minutes?
steps: After 5 full turns the seat is back at the bottom
2 minutes is half of a turn, so the seat goes from the bottom to the top
example.answer: At the very top of the wheel

learn.reallife: Your heartbeat, the seasons and the tides all follow repeating cycles. Doctors even count heartbeats per minute, which is a frequency!

games.title: Does it repeat?
items: Minute hand of a clock
Phases of the Moon
Swing of a pendulum
Day and night
A ball rolling down a slope and stopping
Growth of a mango tree
Height of a rocket after launch
Burning of a candle

items.q: Pendulum: 30 swings in 60 seconds. Period in seconds?
A wheel turns once in 5 minutes. Turns in 1 hour?
Degrees turned by the minute hand in 20 minutes
Degrees turned by the hour hand in 1 hour
Full turns of the seconds hand in 5 minutes

quiz.q: Which of these is a periodic motion?
options: A leaf falling from a tree
quiz.explain: A pendulum repeats the same back-and-forth swing in equal intervals of time.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any motion is periodic, even one that happens only once

quiz.q: A pendulum completes 20 swings in 40 seconds. What is its period?
quiz.explain: Period = time for one swing = 40 ÷ 20 = 2 seconds.
steps: Period = total time ÷ number of swings
quiz.mistake: Divides the swings by the time, which gives the frequency (0.5) instead

quiz.q: A fan blade completes one turn every 0.25 seconds. How many turns does it make in one second?
quiz.explain: Frequency = 1 ÷ period = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 turns per second.
quiz.mistake: Thinks frequency and period are the same number

quiz.q: A giant wheel takes 6 minutes per turn. Kabir's seat starts at the bottom. Where is it after 33 minutes?
options: A quarter of the way round
quiz.explain: 33 = 5 × 6 + 3. After 5 full turns he is back at the bottom; 3 more minutes is half a turn, which takes him to the top.
steps: Half a turn from the bottom = the top
quiz.mistake: Ignores the remainder and thinks he is back at the start

quiz.q: Through how many degrees does the minute hand of a clock turn in 25 minutes?
quiz.explain: The minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes, which is 6° per minute. 25 × 6° = 150°.
quiz.mistake: Uses 5° per minute, as if a full turn were 300°

quiz.q: Starting at 12:00, through how many degrees has the hour hand turned at 3:00?
quiz.explain: The hour hand turns 360° in 12 hours, which is 30° per hour. In 3 hours it turns 90°.
quiz.mistake: Gives the angle for only one hour

quiz.q: Today is Monday. What day of the week will it be 100 days from today?
quiz.explain: The days of the week repeat with period 7. 100 = 14 × 7 + 2, so it is 2 days after Monday.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to use the remainder, or counts today as day 1

quiz.q: Harpreet records the height of her seat on a giant wheel every few seconds and draws a graph of height against time. What shape does it have?
options: A single hill and then flat
A wave that rises and falls again and again
quiz.explain: The seat goes up and down in every turn, so the graph repeats the same up-and-down shape each period.
quiz.mistake: Thinks height keeps increasing because the wheel keeps moving

teach.ask: Gappu is dizzy from the giant wheel: "What does it mean when you say the wheel's motion is periodic?"
teach.praise: It repeats the same cycle after the same fixed time, called the period. And frequency tells how many cycles in each second. Wheee!
teach.nudge: Does the wheel take the same time for every round? What do we call that time?

learn.hook: Every spoke of a cycle wheel sweeps out angles as it turns. One full turn is 360°, but a wheel can keep turning through 720°, 1080° and beyond!
points: A full turn is 360°, a half turn is 180° and a quarter turn is 90°.
Angles are classified as acute (less than 90°), right (90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°), straight (180°) and reflex (between 180° and 360°).
An angle at the centre of a circle is called a central angle. Equal slices of a circle have equal central angles: n equal slices have 360° ÷ n each.
Arc length for a central angle θ is (θ/360) × 2πr, the same fraction of the full circumference.
Turning anticlockwise is usually taken as positive. Turning through more than 360° just means extra full turns: 450° = 360° + 90°.

example.q: A wheel of radius 35 cm turns through 72°. How far does a point on the rim travel? (Use π = 22/7.)

learn.reallife: A pizza or a birthday cake cut into 8 equal slices gives each slice a central angle of 45°.

quiz.q: A wheel turns through 3/4 of a full turn. What angle is that?
quiz.mistake: Uses 100 for a full turn, as with percentages, giving 75°

quiz.q: What is the smaller angle between the hands of a clock at 4:00?
quiz.explain: The hour hand is on 4 and the minute hand on 12. Each hour mark is 30° apart, so 4 × 30° = 120°.
quiz.mistake: Uses 25° per hour mark, or gives the larger reflex angle 240°

quiz.q: What type of angle is 135°?
quiz.explain: 135° is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it is obtuse.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any angle over 90° is reflex

quiz.q: A spinning top turns through 900°. How can you describe this turn?
options: 2 full turns and a half turn
2 full turns and a quarter turn
quiz.explain: 900° = 2 × 360° + 180°, which is 2 full turns plus a half turn.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 100 instead of 360

quiz.q: In a circle of radius 14 cm, find the length of the arc with a central angle of 90°. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: 90° is a quarter of the circle, so the arc is a quarter of the circumference 88 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses a half instead of a quarter, or forgets to take the fraction at all

quiz.q: Joseph cuts a round cake into 8 equal slices from the centre. What is the angle of each slice at the centre?
quiz.explain: The full angle at the centre is 360°, shared equally among 8 slices: 360° ÷ 8 = 45°.
quiz.mistake: Shares 320° or 480° instead of 360°, or confuses the slice count with the angle

quiz.q: An angle of 110° is marked at a point. What is the reflex angle at that point?
quiz.explain: The angles all the way round a point add to 360°, so the reflex angle is 360° − 110° = 250°.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts from 180°, which gives the supplement instead

quiz.q: Aisha's bicycle wheel makes 5 complete turns. Through what total angle has a spoke turned?
quiz.explain: Each full turn is 360°, so 5 turns is 5 × 360° = 1800°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks angles stop at 360°

teach.ask: Gappu spins round and round: "If I turn all the way round twice, is my angle still 360°?"
teach.praise: One full turn is 360°, so two turns are 720°. And angles can be acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex. My head is spinning, but I get it!
teach.nudge: How many degrees are in one full turn? What happens when you keep turning?

learn.hook: How high is your seat on the giant wheel right now? With an angle and the radius, trigonometry can tell you without a measuring tape!
points: In a right triangle, for an acute angle θ: the hypotenuse is the longest side, the opposite side is across from θ, and the adjacent side is next to θ.
sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent.
For a fixed angle these ratios stay the same however big the triangle is, because all such triangles are similar.
A point on a circle of radius r, at angle θ above the horizontal line through the centre, is r sin θ above the centre and r cos θ across from it. Also sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

example.q: A giant wheel has radius 10 m and its centre is 12 m above the ground. Riya's seat is at 30° above the horizontal line through the centre. How high is she?
steps: Height above the centre = r sin θ = 10 × sin 30°

learn.reallife: Engineers use sine and cosine to design ramps, roofs and giant wheels, and to work out heights of towers they cannot climb.

games.title: Trig true or false
items: For an acute angle in a right triangle, sin θ is never more than 1
The opposite side is always shorter than the hypotenuse, so the ratio is less than 1.
In a bigger triangle with the same angles, sin θ is bigger
All sides grow in the same ratio, so the ratio opposite ÷ hypotenuse stays the same.
In a 30°-60°-90° triangle the side next to 60° is half the hypotenuse.
tan θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse
That is sin θ. tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent.
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
This comes from Pythagoras: opposite² + adjacent² = hypotenuse².
sin 30° + sin 30° = sin 60°
sin 30° + sin 30° = 1, but sin 60° = √3/2 ≈ 0.87. You cannot add angles inside sin like that.

quiz.q: A right triangle has sides 3, 4 and 5. For the angle θ opposite the side 3, what is sin θ?
quiz.explain: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse = 3 ÷ 5.
quiz.mistake: Divides by the adjacent side, which gives tan θ

quiz.q: In the same 3-4-5 triangle, what is tan θ for the angle opposite the side 3?
quiz.explain: tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent = 3 ÷ 4.
quiz.mistake: Turns the ratio upside down

quiz.q: A 10 m ladder leans against a wall, making 30° with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach?
quiz.explain: The height is opposite the 30° angle and the ladder is the hypotenuse. Height = 10 × sin 30° = 10 × 1/2 = 5 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses cos 30° (giving 8.66 m), which is the distance along the ground

quiz.q: What is the value of sin 30°?
quiz.explain: In a 30°-60°-90° triangle the side opposite 30° is half the hypotenuse, so sin 30° = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up sin 30° with sin 60° = √3/2

quiz.q: A giant wheel of radius 8 m has its centre 10 m above the ground. A seat is 30° below the horizontal line through the centre. How high is the seat?
quiz.explain: The seat is 8 × sin 30° = 4 m below the centre, so its height is 10 − 4 = 6 m.
quiz.mistake: Adds the 4 m even though the seat is below the centre

quiz.q: θ is an acute angle with sin θ = 5/13. What is cos θ?
quiz.explain: Draw a right triangle with opposite 5 and hypotenuse 13. The adjacent side is √(169 − 25) = 12, so cos θ = 12/13.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 5 from 13 to get the adjacent side as 8

quiz.q: As θ increases from 0° to 90°, what happens to sin θ?
quiz.explain: sin 0° = 0 and sin 90° = 1. As the angle opens up, the opposite side grows compared with the hypotenuse.
quiz.mistake: Confuses sin θ with cos θ, which decreases from 1 to 0

quiz.q: A ramp rises 1 m for every 2 m measured along its sloping surface. What angle does it make with the ground?
quiz.explain: sin θ = rise ÷ slope length = 1/2, and sin 30° = 1/2, so θ = 30°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a ratio of 1/2 means 45°, or uses cos instead of sin

teach.ask: Gappu looks at a right triangle: "What is this sin θ everyone talks about? Is it a side or an angle?"
teach.praise: sin θ is a ratio: the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse. It stays the same for the same angle, however big the triangle! Brilliant!
teach.nudge: Which two sides of the triangle do you divide to get sin θ?

learn.hook: A farmer in Punjab wants to sow wheat on an odd-shaped field. Break it into triangles and rectangles, and its area is no longer a mystery!
points: Perimeter is the length of the boundary; area is the amount of surface inside, measured in square units such as cm² or m².
Triangle: area = ½ × base × height, where the height is perpendicular to the base.
Parallelogram: area = base × height. Rectangle: length × breadth. Square: side².
Trapezium: area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × distance between them. Rhombus: area = ½ × d₁ × d₂ (product of diagonals).
Any quadrilateral can be split by a diagonal into two triangles; add their areas.

example.q: A field is a trapezium with parallel sides 30 m and 20 m, which are 12 m apart. Find its area.

learn.reallife: Painters, tile-layers and farmers all estimate costs by area: ₹ per square metre of paint, tiles or seeds.

items.q: Triangle: base 10 cm, height 6 cm. Area in cm²?
Parallelogram: base 7 m, height 5 m. Area in m²?
Rhombus: diagonals 6 cm and 8 cm. Area in cm²?
Square of side 12 cm. Area in cm²?
Trapezium: parallel sides 5 and 7, height 4. Area?
Rectangle 15 m by 4 m. Perimeter in m?

quiz.q: Find the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and height 7 cm.
quiz.explain: Area = ½ × 12 × 7 = 42 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ and gets 84

quiz.q: A parallelogram-shaped plot has base 15 m and height 8 m. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Area of a parallelogram = base × height = 15 × 8 = 120 m².
quiz.mistake: Uses ½ as for a triangle, or adds the sides

quiz.q: A rhombus-shaped kite has diagonals 10 cm and 16 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Area of a rhombus = ½ × d₁ × d₂ = ½ × 10 × 16 = 80 cm².
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the diagonals but forgets the ½

quiz.q: A trapezium has parallel sides 9 cm and 13 cm, and the distance between them is 6 cm. Find its area.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½, or uses only the longer parallel side

quiz.q: In quadrilateral ABCD, diagonal AC = 20 m. The perpendiculars from B and D to AC are 6 m and 8 m. Find the area of ABCD.
quiz.explain: AC splits ABCD into two triangles with base 20 m: ½ × 20 × 6 + ½ × 20 × 8 = 60 + 80 = 140 m².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ for each triangle

quiz.q: A rectangular garden has perimeter 36 m and length 10 m. What is its area?
quiz.explain: Length + breadth = 36 ÷ 2 = 18, so breadth = 8 m. Area = 10 × 8 = 80 m².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve the perimeter, so takes breadth as 26

quiz.q: A right triangle has legs 9 cm and 12 cm. What is its area?
quiz.explain: In a right triangle the two legs are perpendicular, so one is the base and the other the height: ½ × 9 × 12 = 54 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½

quiz.q: A triangle has area 60 cm² and base 15 cm. What is its height?
quiz.mistake: Divides 60 by 15 and forgets the ½ in the formula

teach.ask: Gappu has a strange four-sided field: "No formula fits my field. How can I find its area?"
teach.praise: Draw a diagonal to split it into two triangles, find each area with ½ × base × height and add. My field is measured!
teach.nudge: Can you cut the field into shapes you already know? Which shape is easiest?

learn.hook: Over 1900 years ago, Heron of Alexandria found a way to get a triangle's area from its three sides alone. No height needed!
points: Heron's formula is used when you know all three sides a, b, c of a triangle but not its height.
First find the semi-perimeter: s = (a + b + c) ÷ 2.
Area = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)].
For an equilateral triangle of side a, this gives area = (√3/4) × a².
A quadrilateral with a known diagonal can be split into two triangles, and Heron's formula used on each.

example.q: Find the area of a triangle with sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm.

learn.reallife: Surveyors measuring a triangular plot of land can easily measure the three sides with a tape, but not the height across the middle. Heron's formula is perfect for them.

games.title: Heron step by step
items: Measure the three sides a, b and c
Find s = (a + b + c) ÷ 2
Work out s − a, s − b and s − c
Multiply s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)
Take the square root to get the area

quiz.q: What is the semi-perimeter of a triangle with sides 7 cm, 8 cm and 9 cm?
quiz.mistake: Gives the full perimeter instead of half of it

quiz.q: Use Heron's formula to find the area of a triangle with sides 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to take the square root at the end

quiz.q: Find the area of a triangle with sides 9 cm, 10 cm and 17 cm.
quiz.mistake: Stops before taking the square root

quiz.q: Find the area of an equilateral triangle of side 10 cm, correct to two decimal places.
steps: s = 15, s − a = 5 for each side
quiz.mistake: Uses ½ × side × side as if the height equalled the side

quiz.q: An isosceles triangle has sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm. What is its area?
quiz.mistake: Uses ½ × 5 × 6 = 15, taking a slanted side as the height

quiz.q: A triangular park has sides 40 m, 24 m and 32 m. Grass costs ₹5 per m². What is the cost of grassing the park?
quiz.mistake: Gives the area as the cost, or forgets the ½ when finding s

quiz.q: The sides of a triangle are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5 and its perimeter is 36 cm. Find its area.
quiz.explain: The sides are 9, 12 and 15 cm. s = 18, area = √(18 × 9 × 6 × 3) = √2916 = 54 cm².
steps: One part = 36 ÷ 12 = 3 cm, so sides are 9, 12, 15
quiz.mistake: Forgets the square root, or doubles the answer

quiz.q: When is Heron's formula most useful?
options: When the base and height are known
When all three sides are known but the height is not
quiz.explain: Heron's formula needs only the three side lengths, so it works for any triangle when the height is unknown.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Heron's formula only works for special triangles

teach.ask: Gappu measured the three sides of a triangle with string but has no idea of its height: "Can I still find the area?"
teach.praise: Yes! Halve the perimeter to get s, multiply s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c), and take the square root. Heron would be proud!
teach.nudge: What is s, and what do you do with it and the three sides?

learn.hook: A round rangoli, a cricket ground, a bangle: circles are everywhere. Just one number, the radius, decides their size!
points: Circumference (perimeter) of a circle: C = 2πr = πd, where r is the radius and d the diameter.
Area of a circle: A = πr². We often use π = 22/7 or 3.14.
A semicircle has perimeter πr + 2r (the curved part plus the diameter).
Area of a ring (between circles of radii R and r): π(R² − r²).
A sector with central angle θ has area (θ/360) × πr².

example.q: Meena draws a circular rangoli of radius 21 cm. Find the length of its border and its area. (Use π = 22/7.)

learn.reallife: The distance a bicycle moves in one turn of its wheel equals the wheel's circumference. That is how a cycle's odometer counts kilometres.

items.text: Circumference of a circle = 2π × ___
Area of a circle = π × ___
The diameter is ___ the radius
The perimeter of a semicircle is πr + ___
If the radius doubles, the area becomes ___ times as big

quiz.q: Find the circumference of a circle of radius 7 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.mistake: Uses πr (forgetting the 2) or confuses circumference with area

quiz.q: A circular flower bed has radius 21 m. What is its area? (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.mistake: Uses 2πr (the circumference) instead of πr²

quiz.q: A bangle has diameter 7 cm. What is the length of the bangle around? (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.mistake: Treats the diameter as the radius and doubles again

quiz.q: A cycle wheel has radius 35 cm. How far does the cycle move in 10 complete turns of the wheel? (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: One turn = 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 220 cm. Ten turns = 2200 cm = 22 m.
quiz.mistake: Makes a mistake converting centimetres to metres

quiz.q: A ring-shaped path lies between two circles of radii 14 m and 7 m. Find the area of the path. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.mistake: Uses π(R − r)², which gives 154

quiz.q: Find the perimeter of a semicircular protractor of radius 7 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: Perimeter = curved part + straight edge = πr + 2r = 22 + 14 = 36 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the straight diameter

quiz.q: The circumference of a circular plate is 44 cm. What is its area? (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: 2πr = 44 gives r = 7 cm. Then A = 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 154 cm².
quiz.mistake: Takes 44 as the diameter or radius instead of solving for r

quiz.q: A round pizza of radius 21 cm is cut into 6 equal slices. What is the area of one slice? (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: Each slice is a sector with central angle 60°, which is 1/6 of the circle. 1/6 × 1386 = 231 cm².
quiz.mistake: Gives the whole pizza's area, or divides by 12

teach.ask: Gappu has a round roti: "How do I find the length around it and the space it covers? Are they the same thing?"
teach.praise: Around the roti is the circumference 2πr; the space it covers is the area πr². Two different things! Yum.
teach.nudge: Which formula gives the length around the edge, and which gives the space inside?

chapters.title: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability

learn.hook: Before a cricket match the captains toss a coin. Heads or tails? Nobody knows for sure, but maths can still say how likely each one is!
points: A random experiment is an action whose result cannot be predicted for certain, like tossing a coin or rolling a die.
Each possible result is an outcome. The list of all outcomes is the sample space: rolling a die gives {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
An event is a collection of outcomes, such as 'getting an even number' = {2, 4, 6}.
When all outcomes are equally likely, P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of outcomes.
Every probability lies from 0 to 1. A sure event has probability 1; an impossible event has probability 0.

example.q: A die is rolled once. Find the probability of getting a number greater than 4.

learn.reallife: Ludo, snakes and ladders and the cricket toss are all random experiments. Fair dice and coins make the game fair for everyone.

games.title: Sure, impossible or maybe?
items: Getting a number less than 7 on a die
A Tuesday coming right after a Monday
Getting 0 on a normal die
A coin landing heads and tails at once
Rain in Chennai tomorrow
India winning the next cricket match
Getting a 6 on one roll of a die
Picking a vowel from the letters of MANGO

games.title: How many outcomes?
pairs: Pick a day of the week
Pick a month of the year

quiz.q: How many outcomes are in the sample space when a die is rolled once?
quiz.explain: The die can show 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6: six outcomes.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the number of outcomes with the number of rolls

quiz.q: Two coins are tossed together. How many outcomes are there?
quiz.explain: The outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. HT and TH are different because the coins are different.
quiz.mistake: Counts 'one head and one tail' only once, getting 3

quiz.q: Which event is impossible?
options: Getting an odd number on a die
Getting a head on a coin
Getting a number less than 3 on a die
quiz.explain: A normal die only has 1 to 6, so 7 can never come up. Its probability is 0.
quiz.mistake: Confuses an unlikely event with an impossible one

quiz.q: Which number can NOT be a probability?
quiz.explain: A probability is always between 0 and 1, including 0 and 1. 1.2 is more than 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks probabilities can be bigger than 1

quiz.q: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue balls of the same size. One ball is picked without looking. What is P(red)?
quiz.explain: There are 3 + 5 = 8 equally likely balls, and 3 of them are red. P(red) = 3/8.
quiz.mistake: Divides red by blue (3/5) instead of red by the total

quiz.q: A spinner has 4 equal parts coloured red, blue, green and yellow. What is the probability that it does NOT stop on red?
quiz.explain: Three of the four equal parts are not red, so P(not red) = 3/4.
quiz.mistake: Gives P(red) instead of P(not red)

quiz.q: A die is rolled. How many outcomes are in the event 'getting a prime number'?
quiz.explain: The primes from 1 to 6 are 2, 3 and 5. The number 1 is not prime.
quiz.mistake: Counts 1 as a prime number, getting 4

quiz.q: Two coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting exactly one head?
quiz.explain: Of the 4 outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT, two (HT and TH) have exactly one head. P = 2/4 = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks there are only 3 outcomes, so gives 1/3

teach.ask: Gappu holds a die: "What does it mean to say the chance of rolling a 6 is 1/6?"
teach.praise: There are 6 equally likely outcomes and only 1 of them is a 6, so the chance is 1 out of 6. Now I understand dice!
teach.nudge: How many different results can the die show, and are they all equally likely?

learn.hook: Toss a coin 10 times and you might get 7 heads. Toss it 1000 times and the share of heads creeps very close to one half. Let's see why!
points: Experimental (empirical) probability is found by actually doing an experiment many times.
P(E) = number of trials in which E happened ÷ total number of trials.
Different runs of the same experiment can give slightly different results.
As the number of trials grows, the experimental probability usually gets closer to the theoretical probability.
The experimental probabilities of all the outcomes add up to 1, so P(not E) = 1 − P(E).

example.q: Kabir tosses a coin 50 times and gets 28 heads. Find the experimental probability of heads and of tails.

learn.reallife: Weather offices say there is a 70% chance of rain because, on past days with similar conditions, it rained on about 70 out of 100 of them.

items.q: 36 of 120 students walk to school: P(walks)?

games.title: What do experiments tell us?
items: If you repeat an experiment, you always get exactly the same probability
Random results change from run to run, so the experimental probability can change too.
More trials usually give an experimental probability closer to the theoretical value
Over many trials the lucky and unlucky runs balance out.
An experimental probability of 0.4 means the event happened in 40% of the trials
Getting 7 heads in 10 tosses proves the coin is unfair
With so few tosses, 7 heads can happen by chance with a fair coin.
Experimental probabilities of all outcomes add up to 1
Every trial gives exactly one outcome, so the counts add up to the total number of trials.

quiz.q: A coin is tossed 200 times and shows heads 112 times. What is the experimental probability of heads?
quiz.mistake: Uses the theoretical value 0.5 instead of the data

quiz.q: A die is rolled 60 times and a 6 appears 12 times. What is the experimental probability of getting a 6?
quiz.explain: P(6) = 12 ÷ 60 = 1/5. The theoretical value 1/6 is close but not the same.
quiz.mistake: Writes the theoretical probability 1/6 instead of using the experiment's data

quiz.q: In a survey of 40 students, 14 said cricket is their favourite sport. What is the probability that a student picked at random from them likes cricket most?
quiz.mistake: Divides by the number who do not like cricket (26) instead of the total

quiz.q: Harpreet scored 50 or more in 5 of her last 25 matches. What is the experimental probability that she scores 50 or more in a match?
quiz.mistake: Divides 25 by 5, or reads 5 as 0.5

quiz.q: A shop checks 500 bulbs and finds 20 defective. What is the probability that a bulb picked at random is NOT defective?
quiz.explain: Good bulbs = 500 − 20 = 480, so P(not defective) = 480 ÷ 500 = 0.96.
quiz.mistake: Gives P(defective) = 0.04 instead

quiz.q: Aisha rolled a die 30 times: 1 came 4 times, 2 came 6 times, 3 came 5 times, 4 came 3 times, 5 came 7 times and 6 came 5 times. What is the experimental probability of getting a 5?
quiz.explain: 5 came 7 times out of 30 rolls, so P(5) = 7/30.
quiz.mistake: Uses the theoretical 1/6, or divides by the other rolls (23)

quiz.q: Which statement about experimental probability is true?
options: It is always exactly equal to the theoretical probability
It can change when the experiment is repeated
quiz.explain: It comes from actual results, which vary from one run of trials to the next.
quiz.mistake: Thinks experimental and theoretical probability are always the same

quiz.q: From past records, the experimental probability of rain on a July day in a town is 0.35. What is the probability of no rain?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts wrongly or adds instead of subtracting

teach.ask: Gappu tossed a coin 10 times and got 7 heads: "So is the chance of heads 7/10 now? I thought it was 1/2!"
teach.praise: 7/10 is the experimental probability from your 10 trials. With many more tosses it should get closer to 1/2. Clever!
teach.nudge: How did you get 7/10? And what might happen if you tossed the coin 1000 times?

learn.hook: A factory cannot test every single pen it makes. So how does it know how many might be faulty? Probability makes the prediction!
points: Expected number of times an event happens = probability × number of trials.
P(not E) = 1 − P(E), because an event either happens or does not.
The probabilities of all the outcomes of an experiment add up to 1.
A prediction is a good estimate, not a promise: the real count may be a little more or less.
A game is fair when every player has the same probability of winning.

example.q: A factory found 3 faulty pens in a sample of 150. About how many faulty pens should it expect in a batch of 2000?

learn.reallife: Insurance companies, doctors and weather forecasters all use probability from past data to plan for the future.

games.title: From least to most likely
games.prompt: Least likely to most likely (one roll of a die or one coin toss)
items: Getting a 7 on a die
Getting a 6 on a die
Getting a head on a coin
Getting a number greater than 1 on a die
Getting a number less than 7 on a die

quiz.q: The probability of rain on any day in July in a town is 0.3. About how many rainy days should you expect in 30 days of July?
quiz.explain: Expected number = 0.3 × 30 = 9 days.
quiz.mistake: Gives the dry days (21) instead of the rainy days

quiz.q: A fair die is rolled 600 times. About how many times would you expect a 4?
quiz.explain: P(4) = 1/6, so the expected number is 1/6 × 600 = 100.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 4 instead of by the 6 faces

quiz.q: If P(E) = 2/7, what is P(not E)?
quiz.mistake: Thinks P(not E) is the reciprocal of P(E)

quiz.q: Joseph hit a six on 12 of the last 60 balls he faced. About how many sixes should he expect in the next 25 balls?
quiz.explain: P(six) = 12/60 = 0.2. Expected sixes = 0.2 × 25 = 5.
quiz.mistake: Uses the old count 12 without scaling to 25 balls

quiz.q: A spinner can stop on A, B or C. P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.3. What is P(C)?
quiz.explain: All probabilities add to 1, so P(C) = 1 − 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2.
quiz.mistake: Adds P(A) and P(B) and stops there

quiz.q: In a game with one die, Riya wins if it shows 6 and Arjun wins if it shows 1 to 5. Is the game fair?
options: No, Arjun's chance is 5/6 and Riya's is only 1/6
Yes, because a die is fair
quiz.explain: A fair game needs equal chances. Arjun has 5 winning outcomes and Riya has just 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a fair die automatically makes any game fair

quiz.q: Arjun tosses a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. What can he conclude?
options: The next toss must be a tail
The coin may still be fair; 10 tosses are too few to be sure
P(head) for this coin is exactly 0.7 forever
quiz.explain: Small samples vary a lot. A fair coin can easily give 7 heads in 10 tosses. Many more tosses are needed to judge.
quiz.mistake: Believes a short run of results proves something, or that a coin 'remembers' past tosses

quiz.q: A bag has 20 marbles. Kabir picks one, notes its colour and puts it back, 100 times. He gets red 30 times. About how many red marbles are in the bag?
quiz.explain: P(red) ≈ 30/100 = 0.3, so about 0.3 × 20 = 6 of the marbles are red.
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of red picks (30) instead of scaling to the 20 marbles

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: "If the chance of rain is 0.3, how many rainy days should I expect in 30 days? And is it guaranteed?"
teach.praise: Multiply 0.3 by 30 to expect about 9 rainy days, but it is an estimate, not a promise. I'll carry an umbrella anyway!
teach.nudge: How do you turn a probability into an expected number? Is the prediction certain?

chapters.title: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions

learn.hook: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ... Indian poets studied this pattern of rhythms centuries ago, long before it got the name Fibonacci. Can you guess what comes next?
points: A sequence is a list of numbers in a definite order. Each number is a term: a₁ is the first term, a₂ the second, and aₙ the nth term.
A rule for the nth term lets you jump straight to any term. For aₙ = 3n + 2, the 10th term is 3 × 10 + 2 = 32.
A recursive rule builds each term from earlier ones, like the Virahanka–Fibonacci numbers: each term is the sum of the two before it.
Famous sequences: square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, ...; triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, ...; cube numbers 1, 8, 27, 64, ...
Looking at the differences between terms often reveals the rule.

example.q: Find the next term of 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ... and a rule for the nth term.
steps: Differences: 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12

learn.reallife: Seat numbers in a stadium, the rows of dots in a rangoli and the beats in a tabla rhythm all follow sequences.

quiz.q: What is the next term of 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ...?
quiz.explain: The differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12: 30 + 12 = 42.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the last difference (10) the same, getting 40

quiz.explain: Each term is the sum of the two before it: 8 + 13 = 21.
quiz.mistake: Adds a fixed number or doubles instead of adding the last two terms

quiz.q: The nth term of a sequence is aₙ = 3n + 2. What is the 10th term?
quiz.mistake: Writes 3 next to 10 instead of multiplying, or adds instead of multiplying

quiz.q: If aₙ = n² − 1, what is a₅?
quiz.mistake: Computes 2 × 5 − 1 instead of 5² − 1

quiz.q: The triangular numbers are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, ... What is the 7th triangular number?
quiz.explain: The nth triangular number is n(n + 1)/2. For n = 7: 7 × 8 ÷ 2 = 28. Or keep adding: 15 + 6 = 21, 21 + 7 = 28.
quiz.mistake: Stops at the 6th term (21)

quiz.q: A sequence starts with a₁ = 2, and each next term is twice the previous term plus 1. What is a₄?
quiz.mistake: Stops one step early and gives a₃ = 11

quiz.q: Which rule gives the sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...?
quiz.mistake: Tests a rule on one term only instead of checking every term

quiz.q: Meena draws a rangoli with 1 dot in the first row, 3 in the second, 5 in the third and so on. How many dots are there in the first 6 rows altogether?
quiz.explain: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 36. The sum of the first n odd numbers is always n².
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of dots in the 6th row (11) instead of the total

teach.ask: Gappu sees 3, 7, 11, 15, ...: "How can I know what the 50th number will be without writing them all?"
teach.praise: Find the pattern, write a rule using n, then put n = 50. No need to write fifty numbers!
teach.nudge: What is the same between one term and the next? Can you write that as a rule with n?

learn.hook: Saving ₹10 more every week than the week before? Your savings make an arithmetic progression, growing by the same step every time!
points: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a sequence in which each term is got by adding a fixed number d, called the common difference, to the previous term.
d = any term − the term before it. It can be positive, negative or zero.
The nth term of an AP with first term a is aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
To find which term equals a given number, solve a + (n − 1)d = that number for n.
The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d], or n/2 × (first term + last term).

example.q: Find the 15th term of the AP 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

learn.reallife: Auto fares that rise by a fixed amount per km, rows of seats that grow by 2 each row, and monthly EMI schedules are all APs.

items.text: In 5, 9, 13, 17, ... the common difference is ___
In 20, 17, 14, 11, ... the common difference is ___
The nth term of an AP is a + (n − 1) × ___
In the AP 2, 2, 2, 2, ... the common difference is ___
If a = 3 and d = 5, the second term is ___

quiz.q: What is the common difference of the AP 7, 11, 15, 19, ...?
quiz.explain: d = 11 − 7 = 4, and it stays 4 between every pair of terms.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the wrong way round, getting −4

quiz.q: Find the 20th term of the AP 3, 8, 13, ...
quiz.mistake: Uses n × d instead of (n − 1) × d, getting 103

quiz.q: Which of these lists is an AP?
quiz.explain: 5, 2, −1, −4 goes down by 3 each time, so d = −3 is constant.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a decreasing sequence cannot be an AP

quiz.q: Which term of the AP 4, 9, 14, ... is 104?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add 1 at the end, answering 20th

quiz.q: Meena saves ₹50 in week 1 and ₹10 more each week than the week before. How much does she save in week 12?
quiz.mistake: Uses 12 × 10 instead of 11 × 10

quiz.explain: Pair the first and last terms: 1 + 100 = 101, 2 + 99 = 101, ... There are 50 such pairs, so the sum is 50 × 101 = 5050.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve, getting 10100

quiz.q: An AP has first term −6 and common difference 3. What is its 5th term?
quiz.mistake: Uses 5d instead of 4d, getting 9

quiz.q: A hall has 20 seats in the first row and 2 more seats in each next row. How many seats are there in the first 10 rows?
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of seats in the last row (38) instead of the total

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I find the 100th term of 2, 5, 8, 11, ... without counting forever?"
teach.praise: Start with a = 2 and add the common difference 3 exactly 99 times: 2 + 99 × 3 = 299. So quick!
teach.nudge: What do you keep adding? And how many times do you add it to reach the 100th term?

learn.hook: A king once promised a wise man 1 grain of rice on the first chessboard square, 2 on the next, 4 on the next... By the last square it was more rice than the whole world had!
points: A geometric progression (GP) is a sequence in which each term is got by multiplying the previous term by a fixed non-zero number r, called the common ratio.
r = any term ÷ the term before it.
The nth term of a GP with first term a is aₙ = a × r^(n − 1).
If r > 1 the terms grow very fast (doubling, tripling). If 0 < r < 1 they shrink, like a bouncing ball.
An AP grows by adding the same amount; a GP grows by multiplying by the same amount.

example.q: Find the 6th term of the GP 3, 6, 12, 24, ...

learn.reallife: Bacteria doubling every hour, a viral video being shared, and money growing with compound interest all follow geometric progressions.

games.title: GP true or false
items: In a GP, you multiply by the same number each time
That fixed multiplier is the common ratio r.
It adds 2 each time, so it is an AP. 4 ÷ 2 = 2 but 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5.
The common ratio of 81, 27, 9, 3 is 1/3
27 ÷ 81 = 1/3, and every next ratio is also 1/3.
Starting from 1, the GP with r = 2 eventually overtakes the AP with d = 100
Doubling eventually beats adding a fixed amount. The 20th term of the GP is 2¹⁹ = 524288, while the AP's 20th term is only 1901.
The nth term of a GP is a × r × n
It is a × r^(n − 1), a power, not a product with n.

quiz.q: What is the common ratio of the GP 3, 12, 48, 192, ...?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts terms (12 − 3 = 9) as if it were an AP

quiz.q: What is the next term of 5, 10, 20, 40, ...?
quiz.explain: Each term is doubled: 40 × 2 = 80.
quiz.mistake: Adds the last difference (20) instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Find the 6th term of the GP 2, 6, 18, ...
quiz.mistake: Uses r⁴ (getting 162) or r⁶ (getting 1458)

quiz.q: Which of these is a GP?
quiz.explain: Each term is the previous one divided by 3, that is, multiplied by r = 1/3.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a GP must be increasing

quiz.q: A lab starts with 50 bacteria, and the number doubles every hour. How many bacteria are there after 5 hours?
quiz.explain: After 5 doublings: 50 × 2⁵ = 50 × 32 = 1600.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 50 by 5 instead of doubling five times

quiz.q: What is the common ratio of 64, 32, 16, 8, ...?
quiz.explain: r = 32 ÷ 64 = 1/2. The terms halve each time.
quiz.mistake: Divides the earlier term by the later one, getting 2

quiz.q: A ball dropped from 81 m bounces back to 2/3 of its previous height each time. How high does it rise after the 3rd bounce?
quiz.explain: Heights: 81 × 2/3 = 54, then 36, then 24 m.
quiz.mistake: Stops at the 2nd bounce (36 m) or goes one too far (16 m)

quiz.q: Aisha sends a Diwali greeting to 3 friends. Each of them forwards it to 3 new people, and so on. How many new people receive it in round 5?
quiz.explain: Round 1: 3, round 2: 9, round 3: 27, round 4: 81, round 5: 243. That is 3⁵.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 3 × 5 instead of raising 3 to the power 5

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: "2, 4, 6, 8 and 2, 4, 8, 16 both start with 2, 4. Why is one an AP and the other a GP?"
teach.praise: In an AP you add the same number each time; in a GP you multiply by the same number each time. 2, 4, 6, 8 adds 2, but 2, 4, 8, 16 doubles!
teach.nudge: From 4 to the next term, did you add something or multiply by something?

learn.hook: 'Mangoes are the best fruit' starts an argument. '7 is a prime number' ends one. Maths loves sentences that are clearly true or clearly false!
points: A proposition (mathematical statement) is a sentence that is either true or false, but not both.
Questions, commands, exclamations and opinions are not propositions: 'Is 5 odd?', 'Shut the door', 'Maths is fun'.
A sentence like x + 3 = 7 is an open sentence: it becomes true or false only once x is known.
Many propositions have the form 'If P, then Q'. P is the hypothesis and Q is the conclusion.
A statement about ALL cases is false if even one counterexample exists. The negation of 'All birds can fly' is 'Some birds cannot fly' (not 'No birds can fly').

example.q: Is 'Every odd number is prime' a proposition? Is it true?
steps: It makes a clear claim that is either true or false, so it is a proposition
Test: 9 is odd, but 9 = 3 × 3 is not prime
One counterexample is enough, so the statement is false
example.answer: It is a proposition, and it is false (counterexample: 9)

learn.reallife: Courts, contracts and computer programs all rely on statements that must be clearly true or false. 'If the PIN is correct, then open the account' is a proposition in code!

games.title: Proposition or not?
items: 7 is a prime number
The sum of the angles of a triangle is 200°
Every square is a rectangle
Is 15 divisible by 3?
Please solve this sum
Cricket is the most exciting sport
What a lovely rangoli!

games.title: Judge the statement
items: Every square is a rectangle
A square has four right angles and opposite sides equal, so it fits the definition of a rectangle.
Every rectangle is a square
A 4 cm by 2 cm rectangle is a counterexample: its sides are not all equal.
2 is the only even prime number
Every other even number is divisible by 2, so it has at least three factors.
The sum of two odd numbers is odd
3 + 5 = 8, which is even. In fact the sum of two odd numbers is always even.
'2 + 2 = 5' is not a proposition because it is false
False sentences are still propositions. A proposition just has to be true or false.
The square of any real number is never negative
Positive × positive and negative × negative are both positive, and 0² = 0.

quiz.q: Which of these is a proposition?
quiz.explain: '7 is a prime number' is definitely true or false (it is true). The others are a command, a question and an opinion.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence with a number in it is a proposition

quiz.q: Which proposition is false?
options: The angles of a triangle add up to 200°
quiz.explain: The angles of a triangle always add up to 180°, so the statement about 200° is false.
