quiz.mistake: Thinks 'every square is a rectangle' is false because squares and rectangles have different names

quiz.q: What is the negation of 'All birds can fly'?
quiz.explain: To deny 'all', you only need at least one exception. Penguins and ostriches show some birds cannot fly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the opposite of 'all' is 'none'

quiz.q: Which number is a counterexample to 'Every odd number is prime'?
quiz.explain: 9 is odd but not prime, since 9 = 3 × 3. A counterexample must satisfy the 'if' part and break the claim.
quiz.mistake: Picks 2, which is prime but not odd, so it does not test the claim

quiz.q: In 'If a number ends in 0, then it is divisible by 5', what is the hypothesis?
quiz.explain: The hypothesis is the 'if' part: a number ends in 0. The conclusion is the 'then' part.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the hypothesis (if part) with the conclusion (then part)

quiz.q: Is 'x + 3 = 7' a proposition?
options: Not on its own; it becomes true or false only once x is known
No, because it has an equals sign
quiz.explain: It is true when x = 4 and false otherwise, so on its own it is an open sentence.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every equation is automatically a true statement

quiz.q: Which whole number is a counterexample to 'n² > n for every whole number n'?
quiz.explain: 1² = 1, which is not greater than 1. (0 also works.) For 3, 5 and 10 the claim holds.
quiz.mistake: Tests only large numbers, where the claim happens to be true

quiz.q: Riya says 'Every rectangle is a square.' Which reply proves her wrong?
options: A 4 cm × 4 cm square is a rectangle
A 4 cm × 2 cm rectangle is not a square
quiz.explain: One rectangle that is not a square is a counterexample, and that is enough to show the claim is false.
quiz.mistake: Gives an example that agrees with the claim, which cannot disprove it

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: "Is 'Laddoos are yummy' a mathematical statement? It sounds true to me!"
teach.praise: A proposition must be clearly true or false, not both. 'Laddoos are yummy' is an opinion, so it isn't one, even if I agree!
teach.nudge: Can everyone agree whether 'laddoos are yummy' is true or false? What must a proposition always be?

learn.hook: 'If you are in Jaipur, you are in Rajasthan' is true. But 'If you are in Rajasthan, you are in Jaipur'? Swapping can change everything!
points: The converse of 'If P, then Q' is 'If Q, then P': the hypothesis and conclusion swap places.
A true statement can have a false converse. 'If a number is divisible by 4, it is even' is true, but 6 is even and not divisible by 4.
Some statements and their converses are both true, such as Pythagoras' theorem and its converse.
When a statement and its converse are both true, we can join them with 'if and only if'.
To show a converse is false, give one counterexample: a case where Q is true but P is false.

example.q: Write the converse of 'If x = 3, then x² = 9' and decide whether it is true.
steps: Swap the parts: 'If x² = 9, then x = 3'
Test x = −3: (−3)² = 9, but x is not 3
example.answer: Converse: If x² = 9, then x = 3. It is false (x = −3).

learn.reallife: 'If it is a mango, it is a fruit' is true, but 'If it is a fruit, it is a mango' would leave the banana seller very upset!

games.title: Match each statement with its converse
pairs: If it rains, the ground gets wet
If the ground gets wet, it rains
If n is divisible by 6, n is divisible by 3
If n is divisible by 3, n is divisible by 6
If a shape is a square, it has four sides
If a shape has four sides, it is a square
If I am in Pune, I am in Maharashtra
If I am in Maharashtra, I am in Pune

games.title: Is the converse true?
items: If x = 5, then 2x = 10
If a triangle has three equal sides, it has three equal angles
If a number is a multiple of 10, it ends in 0
If n is divisible by 6, n is divisible by 3
If a shape is a square, it has four sides
If x = 3, then x² = 9
If I am in Pune, I am in Maharashtra

quiz.q: What is the converse of 'If it is raining, then the ground is wet'?
options: If it is not raining, the ground is not wet
If the ground is wet, then it is raining
If the ground is not wet, it is not raining
It is raining and the ground is wet
quiz.explain: The converse swaps the hypothesis and the conclusion.
quiz.mistake: Adds 'not' to both parts instead of swapping them

quiz.q: 'If a number is divisible by 4, then it is even' is true. What about its converse?
options: True, because 8 is even and divisible by 4
False, because 6 is even but not divisible by 4
quiz.explain: The converse is 'If a number is even, it is divisible by 4'. The even number 6 is not divisible by 4, so the converse is false.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one example that works (like 8) proves a statement for all numbers

quiz.q: Which statement has a TRUE converse?
options: If a quadrilateral is a square, it has four right angles
If a triangle has three equal sides, it has three equal angles
If n is divisible by 6, then n is divisible by 3
quiz.explain: A triangle with three equal angles also has three equal sides, so this converse is true. The others fail: x = −3, a rectangle, and n = 9.
quiz.mistake: Assumes that if a statement is true, its converse must be true too

quiz.q: Which value of x shows that 'If x² = 9, then x = 3' is false?
quiz.explain: (−3)² = 9, so the 'if' part holds, but x is not 3.
quiz.mistake: Picks 3, which agrees with the statement instead of breaking it

quiz.q: 'If two angles are vertically opposite, then they are equal' is true. Is its converse true?
options: Yes, equal angles are always vertically opposite
No, two angles can be equal without being vertically opposite
Yes, but only for right angles
quiz.explain: The converse says 'If two angles are equal, they are vertically opposite'. Two 60° angles in an equilateral triangle are equal but not vertically opposite.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every true statement has a true converse

quiz.q: By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem, which triangle is right-angled?
quiz.explain: 7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25². When the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the longest side, the triangle is right-angled.
steps: Equal, so there is a right angle opposite the side 25
quiz.mistake: Adds the sides instead of their squares

quiz.q: 'A triangle is equilateral if and only if all its angles are 60°.' What does 'if and only if' tell us?
options: Both the statement and its converse are true
quiz.explain: 'If and only if' joins a statement with its converse when both are true.
quiz.mistake: Reads 'if and only if' as just 'if'

quiz.q: 'If n is odd, then n² is odd' is true. Is its converse 'If n² is odd, then n is odd' true?
options: Yes: if n were even, n² would be even, so n must be odd
No: 9 is odd but 3 is not
No: the converse of a true statement is always false
quiz.explain: If n were even, n² = n × n would be even. So whenever n² is odd, n must be odd. Both directions are true.
quiz.mistake: Thinks converses are always false, which is just as wrong as thinking they are always true

teach.ask: Gappu says: "'If it is a parrot, it is a bird' is true. So 'If it is a bird, it is a parrot' must also be true, right?"
teach.praise: The converse swaps the two parts, and it can be false. A crow is a bird but not a parrot! Thanks for saving me from a silly mistake.
teach.nudge: What happens when you swap the 'if' and 'then' parts? Can you think of a bird that is not a parrot?

learn.hook: Kabir checked 100 examples and says his rule always works. A mathematician smiles: 'Show me a proof that covers ALL numbers, even the ones you didn't try!'
points: A proof is a chain of logical steps that shows a statement is true in every case, starting from facts already accepted.
Axioms are basic facts accepted without proof. Theorems are statements that have been proved. A conjecture is believed true but not yet proved.
Checking examples can suggest a pattern, but it can never prove a statement about all numbers.
Use algebra to cover all cases: an even number is 2m and an odd number is 2m + 1, for some integer m.
To disprove a statement about all cases, one counterexample is enough.

example.q: Prove that the sum of two odd numbers is always even.
steps: Let the odd numbers be 2m + 1 and 2n + 1, where m and n are integers
This is 2 times an integer, so it is even, whatever m and n are
example.answer: The sum is 2(m + n + 1), which is always even.

learn.reallife: Online banking is safe because of number facts that mathematicians have proved. Engineers rely on proved results, not lucky guesses, to make bridges stand.

games.title: Prove: odd + odd = even
items: Let the numbers be 2m + 1 and 2n + 1
Add them: 2m + 2n + 2
Take out 2: 2(m + n + 1)
2 times an integer is even, so the sum is even

games.title: Words of proof
pairs: A basic fact accepted without proof
A statement that has been proved
Believed to be true but not yet proved
One case that shows a claim is false
Statement with hypothesis and conclusion swapped

quiz.q: Kabir checks 1 + 3 = 4, 3 + 5 = 8 and 5 + 7 = 12, and says: 'The sum of two odd numbers is always even. Proved!' What is wrong?
options: Nothing, three examples are a proof
Examples alone cannot prove a statement for all numbers
quiz.explain: The statement is true, but checking a few cases is not a proof. A proof must work for every pair of odd numbers, for example using 2m + 1 and 2n + 1.
quiz.mistake: Believes that enough examples make a proof

quiz.q: Which expression stands for any odd number, if m is an integer?
quiz.explain: 2m is always even, so one more than it, 2m + 1, is always odd.
quiz.mistake: Thinks m + 1 is always odd, but it is even when m is odd

quiz.q: The sum of three consecutive integers n, n + 1, n + 2 is 3n + 3. Which number always divides this sum?
quiz.explain: 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1), so the sum is always a multiple of 3. It is not always even: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9.
quiz.mistake: Generalises from 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 and says 6

quiz.q: What do we call a basic fact that is accepted without proof?
quiz.explain: Axioms are the starting points of reasoning; theorems are proved from them.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up theorems (proved) with axioms (assumed)

quiz.q: (2m + 1)(2n + 1) = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1. What does this prove about the product of two odd numbers?
options: It is always a multiple of 4
quiz.explain: 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1, which is one more than an even number, so it is odd.
quiz.mistake: Sees the even terms 4mn, 2m and 2n and forgets the + 1

quiz.q: Goldbach's conjecture says every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes. What is its status?
options: It has been checked for very many numbers but not yet proved
It has been shown false by a counterexample
quiz.explain: Computers have checked it for enormous numbers, but nobody has found a proof yet, so it is still a conjecture.
quiz.mistake: Thinks checking very many cases turns a conjecture into a theorem

quiz.q: How many counterexamples are needed to show that a statement about all numbers is false?
quiz.explain: A claim about ALL cases fails as soon as one case breaks it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks you need many failures to disprove a general claim

quiz.q: In the usual proof that the angles of a triangle add up to 180°, a line is drawn through one vertex parallel to the opposite side. Which fact is used next?
options: Alternate angles made by a transversal with parallel lines are equal
The diagonals of a square are equal
quiz.explain: The two alternate angles equal two angles of the triangle, and together with the third angle they form a straight angle of 180°.
quiz.mistake: Tries to use a special triangle instead of facts that work for every triangle

teach.ask: Gappu tested 50 pairs of even numbers and their sum was always even: "Isn't that a proof?"
teach.praise: Examples are not enough: a proof must cover every case. Using 2m + 2n = 2(m + n) proves it for all even numbers at once!
teach.nudge: What about the numbers you didn't test? How can you show it works for every even number?

learn.hook: Your class has 40 marks scribbled on a page. In two minutes, can you say how many scored above 30? Organise the data and you can!
points: Data are facts or numbers collected for a purpose. Data you collect yourself are primary data; data taken from records or other sources are secondary data.
Raw data are data not yet arranged. Range = highest value − lowest value.
A frequency table shows how often each value (or group of values) occurs. Tally marks help you count.
For large data, use classes like 10–20, 20–30. Class width = upper limit − lower limit; class mark = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2.
In classes such as 10–20 and 20–30, a value of exactly 20 is counted in 20–30 (the lower limit is included).

example.q: Marks of 12 students (out of 20): 12, 15, 8, 18, 15, 11, 9, 15, 17, 12, 6, 14. Make a frequency table with classes 5–10, 10–15, 15–20.

learn.reallife: The Census of India collects data from crores of households and organises it into tables so the government can plan schools, roads and hospitals.

games.title: Data words
pairs: How many times a value occurs

games.title: Primary or secondary data?
items: Heights you measure of your classmates
A survey you run on favourite snacks
Temperatures you record each morning
Your own count of cars passing the school gate
Population figures from the Census website
Rainfall data from a newspaper
Cricket scores from a sports magazine
Exam results published by the school

quiz.q: What is the range of the data 12, 7, 19, 3, 15?
quiz.explain: Range = highest − lowest = 19 − 3 = 16.
quiz.mistake: Gives the highest value instead of the difference

quiz.q: What is the class mark of the class 20–30?
quiz.explain: Class mark = (20 + 30) ÷ 2 = 25, the middle of the class.
quiz.mistake: Gives the class width (10) or the sum of the limits (50)

quiz.q: What is the width of the class 45–60?
quiz.explain: Class width = upper limit − lower limit = 60 − 45 = 15.
quiz.mistake: Gives the class mark (52.5) instead of the width

quiz.q: Test scores of 10 students: 6, 8, 9, 5, 8, 10, 7, 8, 9, 4. How many students scored 8 or more?
quiz.explain: The scores 8 or more are 8, 9, 8, 10, 8 and 9: six students.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the scores above 8, leaving out the 8s

quiz.q: Classes are 0–10, 10–20, 20–30. In which class is a value of exactly 10 counted?
quiz.explain: In these classes the lower limit is included and the upper limit is not, so 10 goes into 10–20.
quiz.mistake: Counts a boundary value twice or in the lower class

quiz.q: Harpreet asks her classmates about their favourite festival and records the answers. What kind of data is this?
quiz.explain: She collected the data herself, first-hand, so it is primary data.
quiz.mistake: Thinks primary data must come from an official source

quiz.q: A frequency table for the number of siblings shows frequencies 5, 8, 12, 7 and 3. How many students were surveyed?
quiz.explain: The total number of students is the sum of the frequencies: 5 + 8 + 12 + 7 + 3 = 35.
quiz.mistake: Gives the largest frequency or the number of rows in the table

quiz.q: Kabir groups heights from 140 cm to 170 cm into classes of width 5 cm (140–145, 145–150, ...). How many classes does he need?
quiz.explain: The data cover 170 − 140 = 30 cm, and 30 ÷ 5 = 6 classes.
quiz.mistake: Counts the boundary points (7) instead of the gaps between them

teach.ask: Gappu has 50 numbers written in a messy list: "How can I make sense of all of them?"
teach.praise: Group the values into classes and count how many fall in each, using tally marks. A neat frequency table at last!
teach.nudge: What could you count to make the list easier to read? Could you put the values into groups?

learn.hook: Your cricket team's scores were 12, 15, 9 and 120. Was the team's 'typical' score really 39? Different averages tell different stories!
points: Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values.
For a frequency table: mean = Σ(f × x) ÷ Σf, where x is each value and f its frequency.
Median: arrange the data in order. For an odd count it is the middle value; for an even count it is the mean of the two middle values.
Mode is the value that occurs most often.
One very large or very small value (an outlier) pulls the mean a lot but hardly changes the median.

example.q: Find the mean and median of 4, 9, 2, 7, 3, 11.

learn.reallife: News reports often give the median house price or median salary, because a few very rich people would push the mean up a lot.

items.text: To find the median, first arrange the data in ___
The value that occurs most often is the ___
Sum of values ÷ number of values gives the ___
One very large value changes the ___ much more than the median

quiz.q: Find the mean of 4, 8, 6, 10 and 7.
quiz.explain: Sum = 35 and there are 5 values, so the mean is 35 ÷ 5 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Gives the sum without dividing, or picks the middle value of the unsorted list

quiz.q: Find the median of 3, 9, 1, 7, 6.
quiz.explain: In order: 1, 3, 6, 7, 9. The middle (3rd) value is 6.
quiz.mistake: Takes the middle of the unsorted list (1) without arranging the data first

quiz.q: Find the median of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.
quiz.explain: There are 6 values, so the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th: (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Picks one of the two middle values instead of their mean

quiz.q: Riya scored 72, 85, 90 and 78 in four tests. What must she score in the fifth test to make her mean exactly 80?
quiz.explain: For a mean of 80 over 5 tests she needs a total of 400. So far she has 325, so she needs 75.
quiz.mistake: Assumes she needs the target mean itself (80) in the last test

quiz.q: What is the mode of 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 3, 5?
quiz.explain: 3 occurs three times, more than any other value.
quiz.mistake: Finds the mean (4) instead of the most frequent value

quiz.q: In a class survey, 4 students have 1 pet, 3 have 2 pets and 3 have 3 pets. What is the mean number of pets?
quiz.mistake: Just averages the values 1, 2, 3 and ignores the frequencies, getting 2

quiz.q: Monthly pocket money of five friends: ₹200, ₹220, ₹250, ₹230 and ₹2000. Which average best shows what is typical?
options: The mean, because it uses every value
The median, because the mean is pulled up by one very large value
quiz.explain: The mean is ₹580, which is more than four of the five friends get. The median ₹230 is much more typical.
quiz.mistake: Always trusts the mean, even when there is an outlier

quiz.q: The mean of 10 numbers is 15. Later it is found that 24 was wrongly copied as 42. What is the correct mean?
quiz.explain: The wrong total is 150. The correct total is 150 − 42 + 24 = 132, so the correct mean is 13.2.
quiz.mistake: Adds the difference of 18 instead of subtracting it, getting 16.8

teach.ask: Gappu has the numbers 5, 1, 9, 3, 7: "How do I find the mean and the median? Aren't they the same thing?"
teach.praise: Mean: add them up and divide by how many (25 ÷ 5 = 5). Median: arrange in order and take the middle one (also 5 here, but not always the same!).
teach.nudge: For the median, what do you do with the numbers before picking the middle one?

learn.hook: A picture is worth a thousand numbers! But a sneaky graph can also trick your eyes. Let's learn to read graphs like a detective.
points: Bar graphs show separate categories with bars of equal width and equal gaps between them.
A histogram shows grouped (continuous) data. The bars touch each other because the classes have no gaps.
If the classes in a histogram have unequal widths, adjust the heights so that the area of each bar is proportional to its frequency.
A frequency polygon is made by joining the mid-points (class marks) of the tops of the histogram bars with straight lines.
Line graphs show change over time. Always check the scale: an axis that does not start at 0 can make small differences look huge.

example.q: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–40 have frequencies 6, 9 and 12. What heights should the histogram bars have if a width of 10 is the standard?
steps: 0–10 and 10–20 have width 10, so heights stay 6 and 9
20–40 has width 20, twice the standard width

learn.reallife: Weather reports use line graphs for temperature, election coverage uses bar graphs, and doctors use histograms of patients' ages.

games.title: Pick the right graph
pairs: Temperature every hour of a day
Joining class marks of a histogram

games.title: Graph detective
items: In a histogram, there are no gaps between the bars
The classes are continuous, so each bar starts where the previous one ends.
In a bar graph the bars may have different widths
Bar graphs use equal widths so only the heights matter.
A frequency polygon joins the class marks of the bar tops
Each point is plotted at the middle of its class.
A graph whose vertical axis starts at 90 can make a small difference look big
Cutting off the bottom of the bars exaggerates the difference between them.
A line graph is the best way to show the favourite colours of a class
Favourite colours are separate categories, so a bar graph suits them better.

quiz.q: Why do the bars of a histogram touch each other?
options: To save space on the page
Because the classes are continuous with no gaps between them
Because it is a line graph
quiz.explain: In a histogram each class ends exactly where the next one begins, so the bars sit side by side.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a histogram is just a bar graph drawn closer together

quiz.q: In a frequency polygon, each frequency is plotted against which value of its class?
quiz.explain: The points of a frequency polygon are at the class marks, the middle of each class.
quiz.mistake: Plots each point at the start of the class

quiz.q: Tickets sold at a school fair: Mon 20, Tue 35, Wed 15, Thu 40, Fri 30. What is the difference between the highest and lowest day's sales?
quiz.explain: Highest is Thursday (40) and lowest is Wednesday (15): 40 − 15 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Uses Monday as the lowest because it comes first

quiz.q: Monthly rainfall in a town: June 120 mm, July 300 mm, August 240 mm, September 150 mm. In which month was the rainfall exactly twice that of June?
quiz.explain: Twice June's rainfall is 2 × 120 = 240 mm, which is August.
quiz.mistake: Picks the tallest bar (July) without checking the numbers

quiz.q: Which graph is best for showing how the temperature changed hour by hour on a day?
options: A bar graph of favourite colours
quiz.explain: A line graph joins readings taken over time, making rises and falls easy to see.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a histogram, which is for grouped data, not changes over time

quiz.q: A bar graph compares two shops' sales of 92 and 96 sweets, but its vertical axis starts at 90. Why does it look misleading?
options: The bars are the wrong colour
The axis does not start at 0, so a small difference looks very large
quiz.explain: Starting at 90, the bars look like 2 and 6 units tall, so one seems three times the other, though 96 is barely more than 92.
quiz.mistake: Reads only the heights of the bars without checking the scale

quiz.q: In a histogram, class 0–10 has frequency 5 and class 10–30 has frequency 20. Taking width 10 as standard, what should the adjusted height of the 10–30 bar be?
quiz.explain: The class 10–30 is twice the standard width, so its height is halved: 20 × 10 ÷ 20 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Uses the frequency as the height even though the class is wider

quiz.q: A bar graph shows Riya sold 45 laddoos and Meena sold 62 laddoos at the Diwali stall. How many more did Meena sell?
quiz.explain: Difference = 62 − 45 = 17 laddoos.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two bars instead of finding the difference

teach.ask: Gappu looks at two graphs: "Why are the bars in a histogram stuck together, but not in a bar graph?"
teach.praise: A histogram shows continuous classes, so its bars touch. A bar graph shows separate categories, so it has gaps. Got it!
teach.nudge: Is there any gap between the classes 10–20 and 20–30? What about between 'cricket' and 'football'?

learn.hook: A recipe for chai, the steps for long division and the instructions inside your phone's map app have something in common: they are all algorithms!
points: An algorithm is a finite list of clear, step-by-step instructions that solves a problem or completes a task.
A good algorithm has an input (what you start with), an output (the result), and steps that are precise, so anyone following them gets the same result.
It must stop after a finite number of steps.
The order of steps matters: 'add 3, then double' is not the same as 'double, then add 3'.
Algorithms can repeat steps (loops) and make choices (if this, then do that).

example.q: Algorithm: start with a number. If it is even, halve it; if it is odd, multiply by 3 and add 1. Stop when you reach 1. Start with 6. How many steps until you reach 1?

learn.reallife: Railway ticket booking, ATM cash withdrawal and traffic signals all run on algorithms written by programmers.

items: Boil a cup of water in a pan
Add tea leaves and let it boil for a minute
Add milk and sugar and boil again
Strain the chai into a cup
Serve it hot

quiz.q: Which is the best description of an algorithm?
options: A finite list of clear steps that solves a problem
Any computer program, even one that never stops
A list of answers to memorise
quiz.explain: An algorithm must be step-by-step, precise and finite.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only computer code can be an algorithm

quiz.q: Which instruction would be a poor step in an algorithm?
options: Stop when the total is above 100
quiz.explain: 'A little' and 'maybe' are vague; two people could follow this step differently.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice that a step must be precise

quiz.q: Start with 5. Repeat 3 times: double the number and then add 1. What is the result?
quiz.mistake: Stops after two repeats (23) or does one repeat too many (95)

quiz.q: In an algorithm for making chai, what are the inputs?
options: Water, tea leaves, milk and sugar
quiz.explain: Inputs are what the algorithm starts with. The cup of chai is the output.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the input with the output

quiz.q: Use the rule: if even, halve it; if odd, multiply by 3 and add 1; stop at 1. Starting from 12, how many steps until you reach 1?
quiz.mistake: Counts the numbers in the chain (10) instead of the steps between them

quiz.q: Why must an algorithm have a finite number of steps?
options: So that it fits on one page
So that it eventually stops and gives an answer
Because computers can only count to 100
quiz.explain: A procedure that never stops can never give an output.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the length limit is about writing space

quiz.q: Algorithm A: add 3, then multiply by 2. Algorithm B: multiply by 2, then add 3. Both start with 5. What is A's result minus B's result?
quiz.explain: A gives (5 + 3) × 2 = 16. B gives 5 × 2 + 3 = 13. 16 − 13 = 3, so order matters.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the order of steps does not change the result

quiz.q: To find the largest number in a list, keep a 'biggest so far' and replace it only when a number is BIGGER. For the list 7, 3, 12, 9, 12, 5, how many times is 'biggest so far' replaced after starting with 7?
quiz.explain: Only the first 12 is bigger than 7. The second 12 is equal, not bigger, so no change.
quiz.mistake: Replaces the value when a number is equal, counting 2

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "My mum's recipe says 'cook till done'. Is that an algorithm?"
teach.praise: An algorithm needs clear, precise steps in the right order that finish with an answer. 'Till done' is too vague for a computer!
teach.nudge: Would two different people understand 'cook till done' in exactly the same way? What makes a step good?

learn.hook: Over 2000 years ago Euclid found a way to get the HCF of two huge numbers without listing a single factor. It is still used in every computer today!
points: Division algorithm: for whole numbers a and b > 0, a = b × q + r with 0 ≤ r < b.

Euclid's algorithm for HCF(a, b): divide the larger by the smaller, then replace the pair by (smaller, remainder). Repeat until the remainder is 0; the last non-zero remainder (the last divisor) is the HCF.
LCM(a, b) = a × b ÷ HCF(a, b).
To test if n is prime, you only need to try dividing by primes up to √n.
The Sieve of Eratosthenes finds all primes up to a limit by crossing out multiples of 2, 3, 5, 7, ... Binary search finds an item in a sorted list by halving the search area each time.

example.q: Use Euclid's algorithm to find HCF(252, 105).
steps: The remainder is 0, so the HCF is the last divisor, 21

learn.reallife: Online payments are kept safe by codes that use Euclid's algorithm and prime numbers. Searching a contact on your phone uses ideas like binary search.

games.title: Euclid's algorithm for HCF(84, 36)
items: Now divide 36 by the remainder 12
The remainder is 0, so HCF = 12

quiz.q: Use Euclid's algorithm to find HCF(48, 18).
quiz.mistake: Stops early and gives the first remainder (12)

quiz.q: Find HCF(91, 65) using Euclid's algorithm.
quiz.mistake: Gives a remainder from the middle of the process instead of the last divisor

quiz.q: To check whether 97 is prime, what is the largest prime you need to try dividing by?
quiz.explain: √97 is a little less than 10, so you only need to try 2, 3, 5 and 7. None divides 97, so 97 is prime.
quiz.mistake: Thinks you must try every number up to half of 97

quiz.q: Riya thinks of a number from 1 to 100. Arjun always guesses the middle of the remaining range and is told 'higher' or 'lower'. What is the most guesses he will ever need?
quiz.explain: After each wrong guess at most half of the numbers are left: 100 → 50 → 25 → 12 → 6 → 3 → 1. After 6 guesses only one number can remain, so the 7th guess is sure to be right (2⁷ = 128 ≥ 100).
quiz.mistake: Thinks you might need to try every number one by one

quiz.q: HCF(12, 18) = 6. What is LCM(12, 18)?
quiz.mistake: Gives the product 216 without dividing by the HCF

quiz.q: After using the Sieve of Eratosthenes on the numbers 1 to 100, how many primes are left?
quiz.explain: Crossing out 1 and the multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7 (but not those primes themselves) leaves exactly 25 primes up to 100.
quiz.mistake: Thinks half the numbers (all the odd ones) are prime

quiz.q: Use repeated subtraction (the older form of Euclid's method) for HCF(35, 14): keep subtracting the smaller from the larger. What is the HCF?
quiz.explain: (35, 14) → (21, 14) → (7, 14) → (7, 7). When the two numbers are equal, that number, 7, is the HCF.
quiz.mistake: Stops after the first subtraction

quiz.q: Write 157 = 12 × q + r with 0 ≤ r < 12. What is r?
quiz.explain: 12 × 13 = 156, so 157 = 12 × 13 + 1. The remainder is 1.
quiz.mistake: Gives the quotient (13) instead of the remainder

teach.ask: Gappu wants the HCF of 1071 and 462: "Listing all their factors will take forever! Is there a faster way?"
teach.praise: Euclid's algorithm: divide, take the remainder, and repeat with the smaller numbers until the remainder is 0. The last divisor is the HCF. It is 21!
teach.nudge: What do you do with the remainder after the first division? When do you stop?

learn.hook: Before a robot vacuum cleans your room, someone had to think like a computer: break the job into tiny steps, repeat them and make decisions. That is algorithmic thinking!
points: Decomposition: break a big problem into smaller parts that are easier to solve.
Loops repeat a set of steps, either a fixed number of times or while a condition is true.
Conditions (if... else...) let an algorithm choose between different steps.
Flowcharts show algorithms as pictures: ovals for start and stop, rectangles for actions, diamonds for decisions (yes/no questions), and arrows for the order.
Efficiency: different algorithms can solve the same problem in very different numbers of steps. Tracing an algorithm step by step helps you find and fix bugs.

example.q: Trace this algorithm: set x = 1. While x is less than 50, replace x by 3 × x. Output x.
steps: 81 is not less than 50, so stop and output 81

learn.reallife: Indian Railways' route planning, Diwali light patterns on a timer and video games all use loops and conditions.

items.text: Breaking a big task into smaller tasks is called ___
A set of steps that repeats is called a ___
A mistake in an algorithm is often called a ___
'If marks ≥ 33, print Pass, else print Fail' is an example of a ___

quiz.q: In a flowchart, what does a diamond-shaped box show?
quiz.explain: A diamond holds a question, and the flow splits into 'yes' and 'no' paths.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the decision box with the action box

quiz.q: A total starts at 10. A loop runs 5 times, and each time it adds 4 to the total. What is the final total?
quiz.explain: 5 additions of 4 add 20, so the total becomes 10 + 20 = 30.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the starting value of 10

quiz.q: Set x = 2. While x is less than 100, replace x by x × x. What is the output?
quiz.explain: 2 → 4 → 16 → 256. 16 is still less than 100, so the loop runs once more, giving 256.
quiz.mistake: Stops at 16, forgetting to check the condition one more time

quiz.q: Which algorithm finds 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 1000 in the fewest steps?
options: Add the numbers one by one
quiz.explain: The formula needs just a multiplication and a division: 1000 × 1001 ÷ 2 = 500500, instead of 999 additions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every correct method is equally efficient

quiz.q: An algorithm says: 'If marks are 33 or more, print Pass; else print Fail.' Meena scores exactly 33. What is printed?
quiz.explain: 33 or more includes 33 itself, so the condition is true and Pass is printed.
quiz.mistake: Reads 'or more' as 'more than'

quiz.q: Harpreet's algorithm for the average of three numbers says: 'Add them, then divide by 2.' What is the correct average of 6, 9 and 12?
quiz.explain: The bug is dividing by 2. The correct average is (6 + 9 + 12) ÷ 3 = 27 ÷ 3 = 9.
steps: Divide by 3, the number of values
quiz.mistake: Follows the buggy step and gets 13.5

quiz.q: What is it called when you break a big problem, like planning a school trip, into smaller tasks?
quiz.explain: Decomposition means splitting a problem into parts: booking a bus, collecting money, planning food, and so on.
quiz.mistake: Confuses decomposition with repetition (looping)

quiz.q: For each of 4 rows, Kabir's algorithm says 'place 6 diyas'. How many times is a diya placed in total?
quiz.explain: The inner step runs 6 times for each of the 4 rows: 4 × 6 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Adds the loop counts instead of multiplying

teach.ask: Gappu wants to teach a robot to water 10 plants: "Do I really have to write 'water the plant' ten times?"
teach.praise: Use a loop: repeat 'water the plant and move on' 10 times, or until no plants are left. Smart robot, smarter bird!
teach.nudge: Is there a way to tell the robot to do the same step again and again? How will it know when to stop?

learn.hook: Kites in the Makar Sankranti sky, carrom boards and window panes are all quadrilaterals, but they belong to different branches of one big family!
points: A quadrilateral has 4 sides, 4 angles, 4 vertices and 2 diagonals. Its interior angles always add up to 360°, because a diagonal splits it into two triangles.
Trapezium: a pair of opposite sides parallel. Parallelogram: both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
Rectangle: a parallelogram with all angles 90°. Rhombus: a parallelogram with all sides equal. Square: both a rectangle and a rhombus.
Kite: two pairs of equal adjacent sides; its diagonals are perpendicular.
So every square is a rectangle and a rhombus, and every rectangle and rhombus is a parallelogram, but not the other way round.

example.q: The angles of a quadrilateral are x, x + 10°, x + 20° and x + 30°. Find all four angles.

learn.reallife: Engineers use parallelogram shapes in car jacks and folding gates, because they can change shape while opposite sides stay parallel.

games.title: Family facts

A square has all four sides equal, which is what a rhombus needs.
Every rhombus is a square
A rhombus can have angles like 60° and 120°, so it need not be a square.
Every rectangle is a parallelogram
A rectangle has both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
A square is a parallelogram
Both pairs of opposite sides of a square are parallel.
The angles of any quadrilateral add up to 180°
They add up to 360°: a diagonal makes two triangles of 180° each.
The diagonals of a kite are perpendicular
The long diagonal of a kite is a line of symmetry that cuts the other diagonal at right angles.

games.title: Name the quadrilateral
pairs: Both pairs of opposite sides parallel
Two pairs of equal adjacent sides

quiz.q: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 80°, 95° and 110°. What is the fourth angle?
quiz.explain: The angles add up to 360°, so the fourth angle is 360° − (80° + 95° + 110°) = 360° − 285° = 75°.
quiz.mistake: Uses 180° or makes an addition slip

quiz.q: The angles of a quadrilateral are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3 : 4. What is the largest angle?
quiz.explain: There are 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 parts, so one part is 36°. The largest angle is 4 × 36° = 144°.
quiz.mistake: Divides 180° instead of 360° into the parts, getting 72°

quiz.q: Which statement is always true?
quiz.explain: A square has four equal sides, so it is a special rhombus. The others are true only sometimes.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the family tree: a square is a rhombus, but a rhombus need not be a square

quiz.q: A quadrilateral has exactly one pair of parallel sides. What is it?
quiz.explain: A quadrilateral with only one pair of parallel sides is a trapezium. Parallelograms and rhombuses have two pairs.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any shape with parallel sides is a parallelogram

quiz.q: Which quadrilateral has two pairs of equal adjacent sides and diagonals that cross at right angles, but need not have parallel sides?
quiz.explain: That is a kite, like the ones flown on Makar Sankranti.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a kite with a rhombus or parallelogram

quiz.q: A rhombus has equal diagonals. What special quadrilateral is it?
quiz.explain: A parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle. A rhombus that is also a rectangle is a square.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the diagonals of a rhombus can never be equal

quiz.q: What is the sum of the exterior angles of a convex quadrilateral, taking one at each vertex?
quiz.explain: Walking once round any convex polygon you turn through one full turn, 360°.
quiz.mistake: Confuses exterior angles with the sum of interior angles of a triangle

quiz.q: The angles of a quadrilateral are x, x + 10°, x + 20° and x + 30°. What is the largest angle?
quiz.explain: 4x + 60° = 360°, so x = 75°. The largest angle is x + 30° = 105°.
quiz.mistake: Gives x (75°) instead of the largest angle

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: "My teacher says a square is a rectangle. But they have different names! How can that be?"
teach.praise: A rectangle just needs four right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel. A square has all that, so it is a special kind of rectangle!
teach.nudge: What does a shape need to be called a rectangle? Does a square have those things?

learn.hook: Push the top of a folding gate sideways: it leans, but opposite sides stay equal and parallel. That's the parallelogram's superpower!
points: A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles.
In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and opposite angles are equal.
Adjacent angles are supplementary: they add up to 180° (co-interior angles between parallel lines).
The diagonals bisect each other: they cut each other into two equal halves.

A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if any one of these holds: both pairs of opposite sides equal, both pairs of opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other, or one pair of opposite sides is both equal and parallel. In a rectangle the diagonals are also equal; in a rhombus they are also perpendicular.

example.q: In parallelogram PQRS, ∠P = 65°. Find the other three angles.

learn.reallife: Table lamps with folding arms, the scissor lift used by electricians and many bridge frames rely on parallelogram properties.

quiz.q: One angle of a parallelogram is 70°. What is the size of an angle next to it?
quiz.explain: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary: 180° − 70° = 110°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all angles of a parallelogram are equal, or subtracts from 90°

quiz.q: In parallelogram ABCD the diagonals meet at O, and AC = 16 cm. What is AO?
quiz.explain: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so AO = 16 ÷ 2 = 8 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that bisect means cut into two equal halves

quiz.q: A parallelogram has sides 9 cm and 6 cm. What is its perimeter?
quiz.explain: Opposite sides are equal, so the perimeter is 2 × (9 + 6) = 30 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds only two sides, or multiplies the sides

quiz.q: Two opposite angles of a parallelogram are (3x − 10)° and (2x + 20)°. What is the size of each of these angles?
quiz.explain: Opposite angles are equal: 3x − 10 = 2x + 20, so x = 30. Each angle is 3 × 30 − 10 = 80°.
quiz.mistake: Gives x (30) as the angle, or uses supplementary angles by mistake

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT always true for a parallelogram?
quiz.explain: Equal diagonals happen only when the parallelogram is a rectangle (or square).
quiz.mistake: Assumes rectangle properties hold for every parallelogram

quiz.q: The diagonals of a rhombus are 12 cm and 16 cm. What is the length of each side?
quiz.explain: The diagonals bisect each other at right angles, making right triangles with legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Side = √(36 + 64) = 10 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the whole diagonals instead of their halves, getting 20 cm

quiz.q: Which condition guarantees that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram?
options: One pair of opposite sides is equal
One pair of opposite sides is both equal and parallel
quiz.explain: If one pair of opposite sides is equal AND parallel, the quadrilateral must be a parallelogram. Just equal is not enough: an isosceles trapezium has one pair of equal opposite sides.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one pair of equal sides is enough

quiz.q: Two adjacent angles of a parallelogram are in the ratio 2 : 3. What is the smaller angle?
quiz.explain: Adjacent angles add to 180°. 180° ÷ 5 = 36°, so the angles are 72° and 108°.
quiz.mistake: Divides 360° into the parts as if they were all four angles

teach.ask: Gappu draws a slanted four-sided shape: "How can I be sure this is a parallelogram, and what do I get for free if it is?"
teach.praise: If both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, then opposite sides and angles are equal, and the diagonals bisect each other. So many free facts!
teach.nudge: What can you say about the opposite sides? And what happens where the diagonals cross?

learn.hook: Join the middles of two sides of any triangle and something magical appears: a line exactly parallel to the third side and exactly half as long!
points: Mid-point theorem: the segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and is half of it.
If D and E are mid-points of AB and AC in triangle ABC, then DE ∥ BC and DE = ½ BC.
Converse: a line through the mid-point of one side of a triangle, parallel to another side, bisects the third side.
Joining the mid-points of the three sides makes 4 congruent triangles, each with ¼ of the area of the original.
Joining the mid-points of the sides of ANY quadrilateral, in order, always gives a parallelogram.

example.q: In triangle ABC, AB = 8 cm, BC = 10 cm and CA = 12 cm. D, E and F are the mid-points of AB, BC and CA. Find the perimeter of triangle DEF.
steps: By the mid-point theorem, each side of DEF is half of a side of ABC
DE = ½ CA = 6, EF = ½ AB = 4, FD = ½ BC = 5

learn.reallife: Carpenters use the mid-point idea to fix a cross-bar exactly halfway up a triangular roof frame, knowing it will be level and half the width of the base.

games.title: Prove the mid-point theorem
games.prompt: D, E are mid-points of AB, AC. Put the proof in order.
items: Extend DE to F so that EF = DE, and join CF
Triangles ADE and CFE are congruent (SAS), so CF = AD = DB and CF ∥ AB
So DBCF is a parallelogram
Hence DF ∥ BC and DF = BC
Since DE = ½ DF, DE = ½ BC and DE ∥ BC

items.q: BC = 18 cm. Length of DE joining mid-points of AB and AC (cm)?
Triangle perimeter 40 cm. Perimeter of mid-point triangle (cm)?

Number of congruent triangles formed by joining all three mid-points

quiz.q: In triangle ABC, D and E are the mid-points of AB and AC, and BC = 14 cm. What is DE?
quiz.explain: By the mid-point theorem, DE = ½ BC = 7 cm.
quiz.mistake: Doubles instead of halving

quiz.q: D and E are the mid-points of AB and AC of triangle ABC. If DE = 4.5 cm, what is BC?
quiz.explain: DE is half of BC, so BC = 2 × 4.5 = 9 cm.
quiz.mistake: Halves DE again instead of doubling it

quiz.q: A triangle has sides 8 cm, 10 cm and 12 cm. What is the perimeter of the triangle formed by joining the mid-points of its sides?
quiz.explain: Each side of the new triangle is half of a side of the old one, so its perimeter is ½ × 30 = 15 cm.
quiz.mistake: Gives the original perimeter

quiz.q: D and E are the mid-points of AB and AC in triangle ABC. DE is parallel to which side?
quiz.explain: The segment joining the mid-points of two sides is parallel to the third side, BC.
quiz.mistake: Thinks DE is parallel to one of the sides it touches

quiz.q: In triangle ABC, a line through the mid-point of AB is drawn parallel to BC. Where does it meet AC?
options: One-third of the way from A
quiz.explain: By the converse of the mid-point theorem, the line bisects AC.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the meeting point depends on the triangle's shape

quiz.q: Aisha joins the mid-points of the sides of an irregular quadrilateral, in order. What shape does she always get?
quiz.explain: Each pair of opposite sides of the new shape is parallel to (and half of) the same diagonal, so it is always a parallelogram.
quiz.mistake: Expects a square because the shape looks neat

quiz.q: The diagonals of a rectangle are 10 cm long. What is the perimeter of the quadrilateral formed by joining the mid-points of its sides?
quiz.explain: Each side of the new shape is half of a diagonal, so each side is 5 cm. It is a rhombus with perimeter 4 × 5 = 20 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the full diagonal as each side, getting 40 cm

quiz.q: A triangle has area 48 cm². What is the area of the triangle formed by joining the mid-points of its three sides?
quiz.explain: Joining the mid-points makes 4 congruent triangles, so the middle one has ¼ of the area: 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm².
quiz.mistake: Halves the area because the sides are halved

teach.ask: Gappu joins the middles of two sides of a triangle with a straw: "Is there anything special about this straw?"
teach.praise: It is parallel to the third side and exactly half its length. That's the mid-point theorem! My straw is famous.
teach.nudge: Compare the straw with the third side. Which way does it point, and how long is it?

learn.hook: 2 samosas and 3 jalebis cost ₹110. How much is one samosa? There isn't just one answer, until you get more clues!
points: A linear equation in two variables can be written as ax + by + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers and a and b are not both zero.
A solution is an ordered pair (x, y) that makes the equation true. Example: (2, 3) is a solution of 2x + y = 7 because 4 + 3 = 7.
A linear equation in two variables has infinitely many solutions: choose any x, then work out y.
To check a pair, substitute both values and see whether the two sides are equal.
An equation like y = 3 can be written in two variables as 0·x + 1·y − 3 = 0.

example.q: Find three solutions of x + 2y = 8.

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers mixing two kinds of sweets in a ₹500 box face a two-variable equation: many different mixes give the same total.

quiz.q: A pen costs ₹x and a notebook costs ₹y. 2 pens and 3 notebooks cost ₹110. Which equation shows this?
quiz.explain: Cost of 2 pens = 2x and of 3 notebooks = 3y. Together: 2x + 3y = 110.

quiz.q: If (k, 2) is a solution of 3x − 2y = 8, what is k?
quiz.explain: Substitute x = k, y = 2: 3k − 4 = 8, so 3k = 12 and k = 4.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 4 instead of adding it, getting 4/3

quiz.q: How many solutions does x + y = 10 have?
quiz.explain: For every value of x there is a matching y = 10 − x, such as (1, 9), (2.5, 7.5), (−3, 13), and so on.
quiz.mistake: Counts only whole-number solutions, or treats it like a one-variable equation

quiz.q: Write 4x − 5y + 6 = 0 in the form ax + by + c = 0. What is b?
quiz.explain: Compare term by term: a = 4, b = −5, c = 6. The sign belongs to the coefficient.
quiz.mistake: Drops the minus sign in front of 5y

quiz.q: For x + 2y = 12, find y when x = 4.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 2, giving y = 8

quiz.q: How can y = 3 be written as a linear equation in two variables?
quiz.explain: The coefficient of x is 0, so x can take any value while y stays 3.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an equation without x cannot have two variables

quiz.q: A box holds 60 sweets: x laddoos and y pedas. Which equation describes the box?
quiz.explain: The numbers of laddoos and pedas together make 60.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the two amounts instead of adding them

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "For x + y = 5, my friend says the answer is (2, 3) and I say (1, 4). Who is right?"
teach.praise: You are both right! Put each pair in and the sum is 5. A two-variable equation has infinitely many solutions. Happy chirps!
teach.nudge: What happens when you put (2, 3) and (1, 4) into x + y? Can an equation like this have more than one answer?

learn.hook: Plot every solution of x + y = 5 and they line up perfectly, like students at assembly. One equation, one straight line!
points: The graph of a linear equation in two variables is a straight line. Every point on the line is a solution, and every solution is a point on the line.
To draw it, find two or three solutions, plot them and join them with a ruler.
x-intercept: put y = 0. y-intercept: put x = 0. These two points are often the easiest to plot.
x = a is a vertical line through (a, 0); y = b is a horizontal line through (0, b).
y = mx (with no constant term) always passes through the origin (0, 0).

example.q: Draw the graph of 2x + 3y = 12.
steps: Plot the three points and join them: one straight line

learn.reallife: A taxi fare chart (fare against distance) or a mobile recharge plan (cost against data) shows up as a straight-line graph.

quiz.explain: Every point has x = 4 and any y, so the points form a vertical line crossing the x-axis at (4, 0).

quiz.explain: On the x-axis y = 0, so 2x = 12 and x = 6. The point is (6, 0).
quiz.mistake: Puts x = 0 instead of y = 0, which gives the y-axis point

quiz.q: Where does the line 2x + 3y = 12 cut the y-axis?
quiz.explain: On the y-axis x = 0, so 3y = 12 and y = 4. The point is (0, 4).
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide 12 by the coefficient of y

quiz.q: Which line passes through the origin?
quiz.explain: Put x = 0 in y = 5x: y = 0, so (0, 0) is on the line. The others do not contain (0, 0).

A horizontal line 2 units below the x-axis

quiz.explain: Every point has y = −2, so the line is horizontal and lies 2 units below the x-axis.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the minus sign

quiz.q: Where do the lines x = 3 and y = −1 meet?
quiz.explain: The meeting point must have x = 3 and y = −1, so it is (3, −1).
quiz.mistake: Writes the coordinates in the wrong order

quiz.q: The line x + y = 6 makes a triangle with the two axes. What is the area of this triangle?
quiz.explain: The line meets the axes at (6, 0) and (0, 6). The triangle has base 6 and height 6, so area = ½ × 6 × 6 = 18.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ in the triangle formula

teach.ask: Gappu has graph paper: "How do I draw the graph of x + y = 4? Do I need lots of points?"
teach.praise: Find two or three solutions like (0, 4), (4, 0) and (2, 2), plot them, and join them with a ruler into a straight line!
teach.nudge: Which pairs (x, y) make x + y = 4 true? What do you do once they are plotted?

learn.hook: One clue gives infinitely many answers. Add a second clue and, usually, just one answer is left. Two lines, one meeting point!
points: Two linear equations in the same two variables form a pair. A solution of the pair must satisfy both equations.
Graphically, the solution is the point where the two lines meet.
Lines that cross give exactly one solution. Parallel lines give no solution. Lines that lie on top of each other (the same line) give infinitely many solutions.
Substitution method: make one variable the subject in one equation and put it into the other.
Elimination method: add or subtract the equations (after multiplying if needed) to remove one variable.

quiz.q: 2 pens and 1 notebook cost ₹50. 1 pen and 1 notebook cost ₹35. What is the cost of one pen?
quiz.explain: Subtract the second bill from the first: the extra pen costs 50 − 35 = ₹15.
quiz.mistake: Gives the notebook's price (₹20) instead of the pen's

quiz.q: How many solutions does the pair y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3 have?
quiz.explain: Both lines have slope 2 but different y-intercepts, so they are parallel and never meet.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every pair of lines must cross somewhere

quiz.q: How many solutions does the pair x + 2y = 4 and 2x + 4y = 8 have?
quiz.explain: The second equation is just the first multiplied by 2, so both describe the same line. Every point on it is a solution.
quiz.mistake: Thinks different-looking equations must be different lines

quiz.q: Solve y = 3x and x + y = 20. What is y?
quiz.explain: Substitute y = 3x: x + 3x = 20, so 4x = 20, x = 5 and y = 15.
quiz.mistake: Gives the value of x (5) instead of y

quiz.q: Kabir is 4 years older than Aisha. The sum of their ages is 30. How old is Aisha?
quiz.explain: Let Aisha be a and Kabir k: k = a + 4 and a + k = 30. So 2a + 4 = 30, a = 13 and Kabir is 17.
quiz.mistake: Gives Kabir's age (17) or just halves 30

quiz.q: On a graph, how do you read off the solution of a pair of linear equations?
options: Where each line cuts the y-axis
The point where the two lines meet
Where each line cuts the x-axis
quiz.explain: Only the meeting point lies on both lines, so only it satisfies both equations.
quiz.mistake: Reads the intercepts of one line instead of the common point

quiz.q: At a zoo, adult tickets cost ₹60 and child tickets ₹40. A group buys 10 tickets for ₹480. How many adult tickets did they buy?
quiz.explain: Let a adults and c children: a + c = 10 and 60a + 40c = 480. Then 60a + 40(10 − a) = 480, so 20a = 80 and a = 4.
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of child tickets (6)

teach.ask: Gappu draws two lines on a graph: "Where is the answer to both equations together?"
teach.praise: The answer is where the two lines meet, because that point is on both. Parallel lines never meet, so then there is no solution. Super!
teach.nudge: Which point is on both lines at once? And what if the lines never meet?

chapters.title: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume

topics.title: Surface area of cuboids, cubes and cylinders

learn.hook: How much paper do you need to gift-wrap a box of sweets for Diwali? That is a surface area question!
points: Surface area is the total area of all the outer faces of a solid, measured in square units.
Cuboid (l × b × h): total surface area = 2(lb + bh + hl). The four walls of a room (lateral surface) = 2(l + b) × h.
Cube of edge a: total surface area = 6a²; lateral surface area = 4a².
Cylinder of radius r and height h: curved surface area = 2πrh; total surface area = 2πr(r + h).
Open shapes (a box without a lid, a pipe without ends) need only the faces that are really there.

example.q: A closed cylindrical tin has radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. How much metal sheet is needed to make it? (Use π = 22/7.)

learn.reallife: Painters charge by the square metre of wall, and tin factories order metal sheets by the surface area of the cans they make.

quiz.q: Arjun paints the four walls of a room 5 m long, 4 m wide and 3 m high at ₹20 per m². What does it cost?
quiz.explain: Area of four walls = 2(5 + 4) × 3 = 54 m². Cost = 54 × 20 = ₹1080.
quiz.mistake: Uses the volume (60 m³) instead of the wall area, getting ₹1200

quiz.q: If the edge of a cube is doubled, what happens to its surface area?
quiz.explain: Surface area is 6a². With edge 2a it becomes 6(2a)² = 24a², which is 4 times 6a².
quiz.mistake: Thinks doubling the edge doubles every measurement, or uses the volume rule (8 times)

quiz.q: A road roller is a cylinder of radius 0.7 m and length 2 m. How much ground does it level in 10 full turns? (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: In one turn it covers its curved surface: 2 × 22/7 × 0.7 × 2 = 8.8 m². In 10 turns: 88 m².
quiz.mistake: Gives the area for just one turn

quiz.q: An open box (no lid) measures 10 cm × 8 cm × 5 cm. What is the area of cardboard needed?
quiz.explain: Four walls: 2(10 + 8) × 5 = 180 cm². Add the base 10 × 8 = 80 cm². Total = 260 cm².
quiz.mistake: Includes the lid (340) or forgets the base (180)

quiz.q: Find the total surface area of a closed cylindrical drum of radius 14 cm and height 6 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.mistake: Finds only the curved surface (528) and forgets the two ends

teach.ask: Gappu wants to cover a gift box with paper: "How do I know how much paper I need?"
teach.praise: Find the area of every face and add them all up. For a box that is 2(lb + bh + hl). Wrapping done!
teach.nudge: How many faces does the box have? What do you do with the area of each one?

topics.title: Surface area of cones and spheres

learn.hook: A birthday cap, an ice-cream cone and a cricket ball: two of these are cones and one is a sphere. How much material covers each?
points: A right circular cone has radius r, height h and slant height l, where l = √(r² + h²).
Curved surface area of a cone = πrl; total surface area = πr(l + r).
Surface area of a sphere of radius r = 4πr².
A hemisphere has curved surface area 2πr² and, with its flat circular face, total surface area 3πr².
If the radius of a sphere doubles, its surface area becomes 4 times as big.

example.q: A conical birthday cap has radius 7 cm and height 24 cm. How much paper is needed for it? (Use π = 22/7.)

learn.reallife: Tent-makers measure canvas for conical tents with πrl, and football manufacturers need 4πr² of leather for each ball.

games.title: Curved surface check
items: The slant height of a cone is always longer than its height
l = √(r² + h²), which is more than h whenever r > 0.
A sphere's surface area is 4 times the area of its biggest circle
The biggest circle has area πr², and the sphere's surface is 4πr².
Curved surface area of a cone = πrh
It uses the slant height l, not the height h: πrl.
Doubling the radius of a ball doubles its surface area
Surface area depends on r², so it becomes 4 times as big.
The curved surface of a hemisphere is half the surface of the full sphere
Half of 4πr² is 2πr².

quiz.q: A cone has radius 7 cm and height 24 cm. What is its slant height?
quiz.mistake: Adds the radius and height directly (31 cm), or forgets the square root

quiz.q: Find the curved surface area of a cone with radius 7 cm and slant height 25 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.mistake: Adds the base area too (704 cm²), which gives the total surface area

quiz.q: Find the surface area of a sphere of radius 7 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: Surface area = 4πr² = 4 × 22/7 × 49 = 616 cm².
quiz.mistake: Uses πr² (154) or 2πr² (308) instead of 4πr²

quiz.q: Find the total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: TSA = curved part + flat circle = 2πr² + πr² = 3πr² = 3 × 22/7 × 49 = 462 cm².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the flat circular face and gives 2πr² = 308

quiz.q: A joker's cap is a cone of radius 7 cm and slant height 12 cm. How much sheet is needed to make it? (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: A cap has no base, so we need only the curved surface: πrl = 22/7 × 7 × 12 = 264 cm².
quiz.mistake: Adds the base circle (418) even though a cap is open at the bottom

quiz.q: A ball has surface area 154 cm². What is its radius? (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.mistake: Uses πr² = 154 (giving r = 7) or forgets the square root (12.25)

quiz.q: A hemispherical bowl has radius 10.5 cm. What is the area of its inner curved surface? (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: Curved surface of a hemisphere = 2πr² = 2 × 22/7 × 10.5 × 10.5 = 693 cm².
quiz.mistake: Uses 4πr² (the whole sphere, 1386) instead of half of it

quiz.q: Find the total surface area of a solid cone with radius 7 cm and slant height 25 cm. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.mistake: Gives only the curved surface (550), forgetting the base

teach.ask: Gappu holds an ice-cream cone: "How much wafer is used to make the cone? Do I use its height?"
teach.praise: Use the slant height l, found by Pythagoras from r and h, and the curved surface is πrl. Wafer-thin and exactly right!
teach.nudge: Is the wafer's length along the side the same as the cone's straight-up height? Which one goes into the formula?

topics.title: Volume of cylinders, cones and spheres

learn.hook: Fill a cone with water three times and pour it into a cylinder of the same base and height: it fills up exactly. Maths predicted it!
points: Volume is the space a solid takes up, measured in cubic units. 1000 cm³ = 1 litre, and 1 m³ = 1000 litres.
Cuboid: V = l × b × h. Cube: V = a³.
Cylinder: V = πr²h (base area × height).
Cone: V = ⅓πr²h, exactly one third of a cylinder with the same base and height.
Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³. Hemisphere: V = (2/3)πr³. When a solid is melted and recast, its volume stays the same.

example.q: A cone-shaped heap of wheat has radius 7 m and height 3 m. Find its volume. (Use π = 22/7.)

learn.reallife: Water tankers, LPG cylinders, ice-cream cones and gol gappas all have volumes that companies calculate with these formulas.

quiz.q: A water tank is a cuboid 2 m long, 1.5 m wide and 1 m deep. How many litres does it hold when full?

teach.ask: Gappu has a cone and a cylinder of the same size base and height: "Which holds more water, and how much more?"
teach.praise: The cylinder holds πr²h, and the cone only ⅓ of that. So it takes three cones to fill the cylinder. Splash!
teach.nudge: How many cones of water do you need to fill the cylinder? What fraction is that?
